cards.title: 1.1.1 Carbohydrates
body: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
The elements are in the of 1 C: 2 H:1 O.
Carbohydrates are obtained from sugar cane, milk, bread, potatoes, wheat, pasta, cereals, “injera” and rice.
Monosaccharides join together to form complex carbohydrate molecules, such as disaccharides and polysaccharides, through the process of condensation.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Proteins
body: **Just as monosaccharides** are the building blocks of polysaccharides, amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
All amino acids contain an amino group (-NH2), which consists of hydrogen and nitrogen.
Proteins are referred to as **nitrogenous compounds**, because of the presence of nitrogen in their structure.
The bond between two amino acids is called a **peptide bond**.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Lipids
body: The most common lipids are fats, oils and waxes.
Like carbohydrates, lipids are composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Fats and oils are similar except that fats are solid, while oils are liquid at room temperature.
Fats produce more energy than carbohydrates or proteins.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Minerals
body: Minerals (mineral salts) are important inorganic compounds containing elements which are essential for normal body metabolism.
Examples of mineral elements are iron, calcium, potassium, etc.
Animals obtain these elements from the foods they take in.
Place a small amount of bean seed in a metal cup (crucible). b.

cards.title: 1.1.5 Vitamins
body: Vitamins are organic substances that are important for normal growth and development.
Vitamins are required in very small amounts (traces) in the diet, but their role is vital.
Vitamins were named A, B, C, D, E and K, in order of their discovery, but they are also given chemical names.
Vitamins do not supply energy nor do they help in building the body.

cards.title: 1.1.6 Water
body: **Water** is the most important nutrient of all living cells.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.
Life on the earth is totally dependent on water.
Water is essential to the existence of living organisms anywhere.

cards.title: Worked example: daily energy needs
cards.problem: An 18-year-old male needs about 14 200 kJ of energy per day. One day he eats breakfast (2 500 kJ), lunch (4 800 kJ) and dinner (4 200 kJ). Has he met his energy requirement? If not, how much more does he need?

steps.text: Step 1: add the energy eaten: 2 500 + 4 800 + 4 200 = 11 500 kJ.
Step 2: compare with the requirement: 14 200 − 11 500 = 2 700 kJ.
Step 3: he is 2 700 kJ short. If this continued, his body would use stored fat (and later protein) for energy and he would lose mass.
Note: an 18-year-old female needs about 9 600 kJ per day; energy needs depend on age, sex, body size and activity.

cards.answer: No — he needs about 2 700 kJ more.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following describes the chemical process of condensation when two glucose molecules are linked?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define condensation**
Condensation is the formation of a larger molecule by releasing a water molecule.
For example, two glucose molecules can be condensed and linked to form one molecule of disaccharide.
**Step 2: Use the chemical equation**
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Condensation}} C_{12}H_{22}O_11 + H_2O$$

cards.answer: The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following organic compounds is defined as 'nitrogenous' due to the consistent presence of nitrogen in its chemical structure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review chemical elements of each compound**
* Carbohydrates (monosaccharides and polysaccharides) contain only Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen ($$\text{C, H, O}$$).
* Lipids contain only Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen ($$\text{C, H, O}$$).
* Proteins contain Carbon, Hydrogen, Oxygen, and Nitrogen ($$\text{C, H, O, N}$$).

**Step 2: Recall the key facts**
Proteins are referred to as nitrogenous compounds, because of the presence of nitrogen in their structure."

**Final Result:**
**Proteins**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary role of the hydrochloric acid (HCl) produced by the gastric glands in the stomach wall?

options.A: To chemically emulsify large fat droplets into tiny lipids.
options.B: To provide an acidic medium (pH 1.5) that activates pepsinogen and kills bacteria.
options.C: To lubricate the lining of the esophagus for peristalsis.
options.D: To neutralize the alkaline bicarbonate ions entering from the pancreas.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze stomach gastric secretions**
the stomach wall secretes gastric juice containing mucus, hydrochloric acid ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH 1.5), and pepsinogen.

**Step 2: Identify the function of HCl**
* It provides an acidic medium (pH of about 1.5) required for the active protease enzyme pepsin to work.
* It activates the precursor **pepsinogen** into the active enzyme **pepsin**.
* It kills bacteria present in the food and dissolves minerals.

**Final Result:**
**To provide an acidic medium (pH 1.5) that activates pepsinogen and kills bacteria.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All biological molecules are organic and should must have
cards.why:
**Logic:**
By definition, **organic molecules** are compounds that contain **carbon** atoms bonded to **hydrogen** atoms (hydrocarbons). While they often contain oxygen, nitrogen, or phosphorus, C and H are the core requirements for a molecule to be considered organic.

**Result:**
Carbon and Hydrogen.

cards.title: Using the energy table
body: Energy from a food = mass of each nutrient (g) × its energy value (kJ/g), added together. Example: 10 g fat gives 10 × 38.0 = 380 kJ, more than twice the energy of 10 g of carbohydrate (171 kJ).

cards.title: Nutrients — what each one is for
body: **Digestion** breaks large insoluble food into small soluble pieces that can cross membranes. Mechanical = teeth, churning, bile emulsifying fat. Chemical = enzymes (each enzyme is picky about substrate and pH).

cards.title: The tube
body: Mouth (amylase on starch) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (acid + pepsin on protein) → small intestine (bile from liver/gall bladder; pancreatic amylase, trypsin, lipase; wall enzymes finish the job; villi absorb) → large intestine (water back into blood) → egestion of faeces.

cards.title: Liver and pancreas are side-offices that dump chemicals into the small intestine. They are not “the tube” itself.
Enzymes by address
body: Mouth = starch. Stomach = protein (needs acid). Small intestine = all three (carb, protein, fat) + bile for fat droplets. “Small intestine does the real absorbing — villi.”

cards.title: More detail — nutrients and the tube
body: Carbohydrates: sugars are already small; starch is a chain that amylase chips into maltose, then maltase finishes glucose. Proteins: pepsin (stomach, pH ~2) and trypsin (intestine, alkaline) cut to peptides, peptidases to amino acids. Fats: bile salts from the liver emulsify (big drops → tiny drops, more surface); lipase then cuts to fatty acids and glycerol. Bile is not an enzyme.

Liver: makes bile, stores glycogen, processes incoming blood from the gut (hepatic portal vein). Pancreas: digestive juice + (later) insulin. Appendix is a dead-end off the caecum — know it exists; don’t invent a major job.

Deficiency sketches: no vitamin C → scurvy; no D / Ca → weak bone; no iron → anaemia; no iodine → goitre (ties to Grade 11 thyroid); no protein in children → wasting. Excess sugar/fat → obesity and later diabetes risk.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Ingestion, Digestion and Egestion
body: The term “soluble” means that a substance can dissolve in a liquid.
**Ingestion** is the act of eating or taking in food through the mouth.
The break down of large food particles into small, usable molecules is called **digestion**.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Mechanical and Chemical Phases of Digestion
body: Most often, the food an animal consumes is in large pieces.
The mechanical phase is only a physical change, because the chemical composition of the food remains the same.
Teeth help in the physical (mechanical) breakdown of food, by biting, crushing and grinding.

cards.title: 1.2.4 The Pharynx
body: The pharynx (throat) is a muscular tube connecting the mouth to the oesophagus (gullet), and the nasal cavity to the trachea (windpipe).
The pharynx is located at the back of the mouth, and transports food to the oesophagus.
The tongue rolls food into small round masses called boluses (singular: bolus).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An 18-year-old male needs about 14 200 kJ per day, but an 18-year-old female needs about 9 600 kJ. What is the main reason for the difference?

options.A: Males usually have a larger body mass with more muscle, so a higher metabolic rate
options.D: Females digest food twice as efficiently

cards.why: Energy needs depend on body size, muscle mass, growth and activity. On average males have a larger body and more muscle tissue, which respires more, so they need more energy each day. Both sexes respire and store fat.

cards.q: Which of the following describes the chemical process of condensation when two glucose molecules are linked?

options.A: The breakdown of a large carbohydrate molecule into two monosaccharides by adding a water molecule.
options.B: The physical chewing and grinding of starch in the oral cavity to increase surface area.
options.C: The reaction of glucose with Benedict's solution at high temperatures to form copper oxide.
options.D: The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define condensation**
condensation is the formation of a larger molecule by releasing a water molecule. For example, two glucose molecules can be condensed and linked to form one molecule of disaccharide.

**Step 2: Use the chemical equation**
$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Condensation}} C_{12}H_{22}O_11 + H_2O$$
This clearly shows two monosaccharides linking to form a larger disaccharide and a water molecule.

**Final Result:**
**The formation of a larger disaccharide molecule by linking two monosaccharides and releasing a water molecule.**

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: Physical change of large droplets of fats in to smaller droplets by bile is:  A) Digestion  B) Peristalsis  C) Emulsification  D) Elimination  E) None

steps.text: **Step 1.** **Emulsification** is the process where bile salts break down large fat globules into smaller droplets.
**Step 2.** This is a **physical change** that increases the surface area for lipase enzymes to act upon.

tips.text: Most animals, particularly humans, need a balanced diet, which should include carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, minerals, vitamins and water.
A balanced diet, obtained from food sources, provides energy, and materials for growth and normal body functioning.

Water should not be thought of as a simple nutrient because it has a wide variety of functions in the body of an organism. It acts as a solvent, is essential in cooling the body, provides a medium of transport and facilitates hydrolysis in all living organisms.
The amount of energy required by a person depends on age, gender, body size and the type of work the person does.
Humans need different minerals and vitamins in their diet for normal body metabolism and food health (well-being).
If we lack one or more mineral nutrients or vitamins in our diet, we can easily suffer from serious deficiency diseases.

questions.q: Which nutrient family supplies $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ of energy and has building blocks that combine one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids?
why: **Identify the energy value.** The energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit) gives the energy yields per gram as carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and water $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$. Since lipids provide exactly double the energy of carbohydrates, the value $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ is the lipid value.

**Identify the building blocks.** The unit states that lipids are made of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acids through condensation reactions, which matches the second clue in the question.

**Check every distractor.** Carbohydrates yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and are built from monosaccharides such as glucose; proteins yield $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and are built from amino acids linked by peptide bonds; water yields $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is built from H and O atoms. None of these matches $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ together with glycerol and three fatty acids.
**Conclude.** Only lipids satisfy both clues, so option C is the single correct answer.

questions.q: Which nutrient family yields $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is built from single sugar units such as glucose?
questions.answer: A. Carbohydrates ($$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, built from monosaccharides such as glucose)
why: **Identify the energy value.** From the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit), carbohydrates give $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and water $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$. The value in the question is therefore the carbohydrate value.

**Match the building blocks.** The unit states that carbohydrates are classified into monosaccharides such as glucose, disaccharides such as sucrose, and polysaccharides such as starch, so single sugar units such as glucose are the building blocks of carbohydrates.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Proteins are built from amino acids, lipids from glycerol and three fatty acids, and water from H and O atoms. None of these consists of single sugar units, so none can be correct.
**Conclude.** Only carbohydrates match both the energy value $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$ and a monosaccharide building block, so the answer is A.

questions.q: Which nutrient yields $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and is confirmed by blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink?
questions.answer: D. Water ($$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, detected by cobalt chloride paper turning from blue to pink)
why: **Identify the zero-energy nutrient.** The energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit) gives water an energy yield of $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, while carbohydrates, proteins and lipids yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ respectively. Water is therefore the only nutrient that releases no energy.
**Match the laboratory test.** The unit states that water is tested with cobalt chloride paper, which turns from blue to pink in the presence of water.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Carbohydrates are tested with Benedict's solution (brick-red precipitate), proteins with the Biuret test (violet colour) and lipids with the ethanol emulsion test (cloudy white emulsion). None of these three uses cobalt chloride paper, and all three yield energy.
**Conclude.** Water alone has an energy yield of $$0.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and turns blue cobalt chloride paper pink, so the answer is D.

In the stomach, gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid at about pH ______(iii)______, which kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen into ______(iv)______, the enzyme that breaks proteins down into polypeptides.
why: **Recall the enzyme of saliva.** The unit states that saliva contains salivary amylase, also called ptyalin, so blank (i) is salivary amylase (ptyalin).
**State the product of starch digestion in the mouth.** Salivary amylase digests starch into the disaccharide maltose at a neutral pH of about 7.0, so blank (ii) is maltose.

questions.q: A student in Asmara eats a lunch of injera with shiro and boiled eggs containing $$80\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$25\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$12\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Using the energy values in the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit) (carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$), calculate the total energy released when this meal is completely oxidized in the body. (b) State which nutrient supplies the greatest amount of energy and give that amount.
questions.answer: (a) The meal releases $$2374\text{ kJ}$$ of energy in total. (b) Carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, $$1368\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** The energy released by a nutrient equals its mass in grams multiplied by its energy yield per gram from the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit), so total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$).
**Calculate the energy from carbohydrates.** Energy from carbohydrates = $$80\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1368\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the energy from proteins.** Energy from proteins = $$25\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 550\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the energy from lipids.** Energy from lipids = $$12\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 456\text{ kJ}$$.
**Add the three values.** Total energy = $$1368\text{ kJ} + 550\text{ kJ} + 456\text{ kJ} = 2374\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the contributions.** The contributions are carbohydrates $$1368\text{ kJ}$$, proteins $$550\text{ kJ}$$ and lipids $$456\text{ kJ}$$. Since $$1368 > 550 > 456$$, carbohydrates supply the greatest amount of energy, even though lipids have the highest energy value per gram, because far more carbohydrate was eaten.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: An evening meal in Keren contains $$45\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$30\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$10\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy this meal can release when completely oxidized. (b) Identify the nutrient that supplies the least energy and state its value.
questions.answer: (a) The meal releases $$1809.5\text{ kJ}$$ in total. (b) Lipids supply the least energy, $$380\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** Total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$), using the energy yields from the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit).
**Calculate the carbohydrate and protein energy.** Carbohydrates: $$45\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 769.5\text{ kJ}$$. Proteins: $$30\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 660\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the lipid energy.** Lipids: $$10\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 380\text{ kJ}$$.
**Add the three values.** Total energy = $$769.5\text{ kJ} + 660\text{ kJ} + 380\text{ kJ} = 1809.5\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare and conclude.** The contributions are carbohydrates $$769.5\text{ kJ}$$, proteins $$660\text{ kJ}$$ and lipids $$380\text{ kJ}$$, so lipids contribute the least energy because only $$10\text{ g}$$ was eaten.

questions.q: A snack sold near a school in Massawa contains $$25\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$10\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy of the snack. (b) Which of these three nutrients has the highest energy value per gram, and what is that value?
questions.answer: (a) The snack contains $$951.5\text{ kJ}$$ of energy. (b) Lipids have the highest energy value per gram, $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** Total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$).
**Calculate the carbohydrate energy.** Carbohydrates: $$25\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 427.5\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the protein and lipid energy.** Proteins: $$10\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 220\text{ kJ}$$. Lipids: $$8\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 304\text{ kJ}$$.
**Add to find the total energy.** Total energy = $$427.5\text{ kJ} + 220\text{ kJ} + 304\text{ kJ} = 951.5\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the energy values per gram.** The values per gram are lipids $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$, proteins $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and carbohydrates $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, so lipids have the highest energy value per gram, which is why only $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipid supplies more energy than $$10\text{ g}$$ of protein.

questions.q: Two students in Massawa compare their breakfasts before a long walk. Breakfast A contains $$60\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$15\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$5\text{ g}$$ of lipids. Breakfast B contains $$50\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$20\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$10\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy that each breakfast can release. (b) State which breakfast supplies more energy and by how many kJ.
questions.answer: (a) Breakfast A releases $$1546\text{ kJ}$$ and Breakfast B releases $$1675\text{ kJ}$$. (b) Breakfast B supplies more energy, by $$129\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** For each breakfast, total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0\text{ kJ/g}$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$), using the energy yields in the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit).
**Calculate the energy of Breakfast A from carbohydrates.** Breakfast A carbohydrates: $$60\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1026\text{ kJ}$$.

**Calculate the remaining energy of Breakfast A.** Breakfast A proteins: $$15\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 330\text{ kJ}$$. Breakfast A lipids: $$5\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 190\text{ kJ}$$.
**Find the total energy of Breakfast A.** Total for A = $$1026\text{ kJ} + 330\text{ kJ} + 190\text{ kJ} = 1546\text{ kJ}$$.

**Find the total energy of Breakfast B.** Breakfast B carbohydrates: $$50\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 855\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$20\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 440\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$10\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 380\text{ kJ}$$. Total for B = $$855\text{ kJ} + 440\text{ kJ} + 380\text{ kJ} = 1675\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the two totals.** Breakfast B gives $$1675\text{ kJ}$$ and Breakfast A gives $$1546\text{ kJ}$$. Difference = $$1675\text{ kJ} - 1546\text{ kJ} = 129\text{ kJ}$$, so Breakfast B supplies more energy by $$129\text{ kJ}$$, because its extra protein and its double-sized lipid portion ($$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$) more than make up for the smaller amount of carbohydrate.

questions.q: Two students compare their afternoon snacks. Snack A contains $$40\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$10\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$8\text{ g}$$ of lipids. Snack B contains $$30\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates, $$15\text{ g}$$ of proteins and $$12\text{ g}$$ of lipids. (a) Calculate the total energy of each snack. (b) Which snack gives more energy, and by how many kJ?
questions.answer: (a) Snack A gives $$1208\text{ kJ}$$ and Snack B gives $$1299\text{ kJ}$$. (b) Snack B gives more energy, by $$91\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** For each snack, total energy = (mass of carbohydrate x $$17.1$$) + (mass of protein x $$22.0$$) + (mass of lipid x $$38.0$$) in kJ.

**Calculate the energy of Snack A.** Carbohydrates: $$40\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 684\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$10\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 220\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$8\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 304\text{ kJ}$$. Total A = $$684 + 220 + 304 = 1208\text{ kJ}$$.

**Calculate the energy of Snack B.** Carbohydrates: $$30\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 513\text{ kJ}$$; proteins: $$15\text{ g} \times 22.0\text{ kJ/g} = 330\text{ kJ}$$; lipids: $$12\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 456\text{ kJ}$$. Total B = $$513 + 330 + 456 = 1299\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the two totals.** Difference = $$1299\text{ kJ} - 1208\text{ kJ} = 91\text{ kJ}$$, so Snack B gives more energy by $$91\text{ kJ}$$, mainly because its lipid content is larger and lipids yield $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$.

questions.q: A nurse in Asmara compares two energy sources for a patient: $$40\text{ g}$$ of lipids eaten as butter and $$80\text{ g}$$ of carbohydrates eaten as bread. Calculate the energy supplied by each food and state which one supplies more energy, and by how many kJ.
questions.answer: The butter supplies $$1520\text{ kJ}$$ and the bread supplies $$1368\text{ kJ}$$, so the butter (lipids) supplies more energy, by $$152\text{ kJ}$$.
why: **State the working principle.** Energy supplied = mass in grams x energy yield per gram. From the energy table (Table 1.1 in this unit), lipids yield $$38.0\text{ kJ/g}$$ and carbohydrates yield $$17.1\text{ kJ/g}$$, so lipids give double the energy of the same mass of carbohydrate.
**Calculate the energy from lipids.** Energy from butter = $$40\text{ g} \times 38.0\text{ kJ/g} = 1520\text{ kJ}$$.
**Calculate the energy from carbohydrates.** Energy from bread = $$80\text{ g} \times 17.1\text{ kJ/g} = 1368\text{ kJ}$$.

**Compare the two values.** Difference = $$1520\text{ kJ} - 1368\text{ kJ} = 152\text{ kJ}$$. Even though the mass of bread is twice the mass of butter, the lipids still supply more energy, which shows why lipids are described as the spare fuel tank of the body.

questions.q: A person eats a meal of fried fish. Describe the complete journey of the fish proteins from the mouth until their digestion products reach the liver. In your answer name each enzyme that acts on the proteins, the pH condition in each region, and the blood vessel that carries the products to the liver.
questions.answer: In the mouth the fish is only chewed and made into a bolus because saliva contains amylase, not a protein enzyme. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which breaks the proteins into polypeptides. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) the pancreatic enzyme trypsin breaks them into peptides, and in the ileum peptidase releases amino acids. The amino acids are absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries and are carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
why: **Mouth and esophagus: mechanical preparation only.** The teeth chew the fish (mastication) and the tongue rolls it into a bolus, which is pushed into the pharynx and moves down the esophagus by peristalsis. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch and not on protein, so no chemical digestion of protein occurs here.

**Stomach: acid activation of pepsin.** Food enters the stomach through the cardiac sphincter. The gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 (about 1.5 to 2.0), mucus and pepsinogen. The acid kills bacteria and activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which hydrolyses the fish proteins into polypeptides, while mucus protects the stomach wall from being corroded or digested.

**Duodenum: alkaline conditions and trypsin.** The partially digested food passes into the duodenum, where bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) neutralizes the acidic chyme and creates an alkaline environment of about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice adds trypsin, which continues the hydrolysis of proteins into shorter peptides.

**Ileum: peptidase and absorption through villi.** Intestinal juice in the ileum contains peptidase, which hydrolyses the peptides into amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed through the single layer of epithelial cells covering the villi into the network of blood capillaries inside each villus; the central lacteal of the villus absorbs fats instead, not amino acids.

**Hepatic portal vein: delivery to the liver.** The capillaries of the villi join to form the hepatic portal vein, which carries the amino acids directly to the liver. The liver acts as a central checkpoint that sorts amino acids, regulates glucose levels and detoxifies harmful chemicals before the blood is distributed to the rest of the body.

questions.q: Describe how the starch in a plate of injera is digested and absorbed from the mouth until the glucose reaches the liver, naming each enzyme involved and stating the pH conditions under which it works.
questions.answer: In the mouth, salivary amylase (ptyalin) at neutral pH (about 7.0) digests starch into maltose. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 denatures salivary amylase so starch digestion stops. In the alkaline duodenum (about pH 8.0) pancreatic amylase digests starch into maltose, and in the ileum maltase digests maltose into glucose, which is absorbed through the villi into blood capillaries of the hepatic portal vein and carried to the liver.
why: **Mouth: salivary amylase at neutral pH.** Chewing with the teeth increases the surface area of the injera, and saliva supplies salivary amylase (ptyalin), which hydrolyses starch into maltose at a neutral pH of about 7.0. The tongue forms a bolus that is swallowed and moved down the esophagus by peristalsis.

**Stomach: the enzyme is denatured.** In the stomach the bolus mixes with gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid at pH 1.5 to 2.0. This extreme acidity denatures salivary amylase, so starch digestion stops completely, and gastric juice contains no enzyme that acts on starch.

**Duodenum: pancreatic amylase in alkaline conditions.** Bile from the liver neutralizes the acidic chyme and makes the duodenum alkaline, about pH 8.0. Pancreatic juice supplies pancreatic amylase, which resumes the hydrolysis of starch into maltose at this optimum alkaline pH.

**Ileum: maltase releases glucose.** Intestinal juice in the ileum contains maltase, which hydrolyses maltose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed through the epithelium of the villi into the blood capillaries inside them.

**Transport to the liver.** The capillaries of the villi drain into the hepatic portal vein, which carries the absorbed glucose directly to the liver, where the glucose level of the blood is regulated before the blood passes to the rest of the body.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Explain how the lipids in a spoonful of butter are digested and absorbed, and name the vessel inside the villus that carries their digestion products away.
questions.answer: No chemical digestion of the butter occurs in the mouth or stomach, only mechanical churning. In the duodenum, bile salts emulsify the large fat droplets into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area, and the alkaline bile also provides the optimum pH for pancreatic lipase, which hydrolyses the fats into fatty acids and glycerol. These products are absorbed into the central lacteal of the villus and are carried away in the lymphatic system.
why: **Mouth and stomach: mechanical treatment only.** Saliva contains salivary amylase, which acts on starch, and gastric juice contains pepsin, which acts on proteins, so neither secretion can chemically digest the butter. The fat is only broken into smaller pieces mechanically by chewing and by churning in the stomach.

**Duodenum: emulsification by bile.** Bile from the liver, stored in the gall bladder, contains no enzymes but contains bile salts. These perform emulsification, physically breaking the large fat droplets into millions of tiny droplets, which greatly increases the surface area available to the enzyme.
**Optimum pH for lipase.** Bile is alkaline, so it neutralizes the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach and creates the alkaline conditions of about pH 8.0 in which pancreatic lipase works best.

**Chemical digestion by pancreatic lipase.** Pancreatic juice supplies lipase, which hydrolyses the emulsified fat into fatty acids and glycerol. This is why bile is essential even though it contains no enzymes: without emulsification the lipase would have far too little surface area on which to act.

**Absorption into the lacteal.** The fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the central lymphatic capillary of the villus called the lacteal, which carries them into the lymphatic system. This differs from the water-soluble products glucose and amino acids, which enter the blood capillaries of the villus and then the hepatic portal vein.

units.title: The Circulatory System
units.intro:
Double circulation: heart → lungs → heart (pulmonary) and heart → body → heart (systemic). Right side is deoxygenated; left is oxygenated. Valves stop back-flow.

Path: body veins → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

lessons.title: The Human Heart and Types of Circulation

cards.title: More detail — heart beat and blood
body: Walls: left ventricle is thickest because it pushes systemic pressure. Atria are thinner receiving rooms. AV valves (tricuspid right, bicuspid/mitral left) stop ventricle-to-atrium backflow. Semilunar valves stop artery-to-ventricle backflow. “Lub-dup” is valves closing.

Heartbeat: atria fill, atria squeeze, ventricles squeeze, pause. Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself — a clot there is a heart attack. Pulse is an artery expanding with each ventricle beat.

Red cells: no nucleus in mature human RBCs, packed with haemoglobin. White cells: some phagocytose, some make antibodies. Platelets are fragments. Plasma is pale yellow. Anaemia = too little haemoglobin or too few RBCs. Clotting needs platelets + plasma factors + calcium; hemophilia is a factor missing.

cards.title: 2.1.1 The Human Heart
body: The heart functions as a pump and is responsible for the circulation of blood through the blood vessels.
The heart produces the pressure responsible for making blood flow through the blood vessels by contracting forcefully.
The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen.
Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the lungs and oxygen diffuses from the lungs into the blood.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Types of Circulation
body: In general, in animals there are two types of circulations: open and closed circulation.
The open type of circulation is found in insects, in which the blood does not flow through blood vessels.
In an open circulatory system, blood pumped by the heart is emptied into large blood-filled spaces.
As the body cells are bathed in blood, materials diffuse out of the blood and into each cell through the cell membrane.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Blood Circuits
body: The pulmonary artery, arising from the right ventricle, divides into two branches, one leading to the right lung and the other to the left.
The oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the four pulmonary veins.
A contraction of the left ventricle pushes blood against the bicuspid valve, closing it, and against the aortic semilunar valve, opening it and allowing blood to enter the aorta.
The blood from all parts of the body returns to the right atrium by way of two large veins.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the primary function of the pericardial fluid present in the pericardial cavity surrounding the heart?

steps.text: **Step 1: Refer to the definition of pericardium and its fluid**
The pericardial fluid present between the pericardium and the heart itself reduces friction between them.
**Step 2: Contrast with incorrect options**
*   Digesting proteins is not a function of pericardial fluid.
* Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid/bicuspid) prevent backflow of blood.

cards.answer: To reduce friction between the pericardium and the contracting heart.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following valves prevents the backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during ventricular contraction (systole)?

steps.text: **Step 1: Locate the valves in each heart chamber**
* The **tricuspid valve** is located between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
* The **bicuspid (mitral) valve** is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
* The **semilunar valves** prevent backflow from the great arteries (aorta and pulmonary artery) into the ventricles.
**Step 2: Identify the valve that matches the question's criteria**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following blood vessels carries deoxygenated blood from the upper regions of the body (head and neck) directly back to the right atrium?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the roles of systemic veins returning to the heart**
The blood from all parts of the body returns to the right atrium by way of two large veins. These are the superior vena cava, which drains blood from regions of the head and neck; and the inferior vena cava, which drains blood from the lower regions of the body."

**Final Result:**
**Superior vena cava**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following structures is absent in healthy human arteries but present in systemic veins to prevent the backward flow of blood under low pressure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare structures of arteries and veins**
* Both arteries and veins have three tissue layers (endothelium, smooth muscle, and elastic/connective tissue).
* Arteries carry blood under high pressure and do not have internal valves.
* Many veins, particularly those in the upper and lower limbs, contain valves all along their length... These valves aid in returning blood to the heart because they open as long as the flow is toward the heart, but close if it is in the opposite direction."

**Final Result:**
**One-way valves**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Blood returning to the heart from the inferior vena cava would enter into the
cards.why: The **inferior vena cava** carries deoxygenated blood from the lower part of the body back to the heart, where it first enters the **right atrium**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: **Bicuspid** and **tricuspid** valves are closed during
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Understand valve function. Bicuspid (mitral) and tricuspid valves are Atrioventricular (AV) valves.
**Step 2:** They prevent backflow from ventricles to atria.
**Step 3:** Therefore, they must close when the ventricles contract (**ventricular systole**) to ensure blood goes into the arteries (Aorta/Pulmonary) instead of back to the atria.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: _____________is a type of circulation, which **purifies** the blood.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand circulation types.** 
- **Systemic circulation:** Carries oxygenated blood to the body and returns deoxygenated blood to the heart.
- **Pulmonary circulation:** Carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs to pick up oxygen and release carbon dioxide (purification).
**Step 2: Conclusion.** Pulmonary circulation is the process that purifies the blood in the lungs.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Arteries
body: The arteries and arterioles conduct blood away from the ventricles of the heart and lead to the capillaries.
The wall of arteries consists of three distinct layers.
The innermost layer is composed of a layer of simple epithelium, called endothelium.
The middle layer makes up the bulk of the arterial wall.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Veins
body: The vessels of the venous system begin with the merging of capillaries into venules.
Venules then combine into small veins and small veins into larger ones.
**Venules** are the microscopic vessels that branch out from the capillaries and merge to form veins.
Around the body organs, blood passes into venules.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Capillaries
body: The pressure of the blood in the capillaries forces fluid out of the capillaries.
Oxygen, glucose and other nutrients diffuse from the blood into the tissue fluid and then into the cells.
Waste products, such as urea and carbon dioxide, diffuse from the cells into the tissue fluid, and then into the blood.
Tissue fluid can also pass into the blood by osmosis, carrying with it dissolved waste products.

Blood plasma constitutes about 55% of the total volume of blood.
By maintaining this balance, plasma is an important agent of homeostasis.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Blood Cells
body: Blood cells, which are formed mostly in the bone marrow, include red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes) and cellular fragments called blood platelets (thrombocytes).
Red Blood Cells (Red Corpuscles) Red blood cells are tiny, biconcave discs that are thin near the centres and thicker around the rim.
Because of its shape, a red blood cell can also deform readily as it squeezes through the narrow passages of capillaries.
When haemoglobin combines with oxygen, the resulting oxyhaemoglobin is bright red, and when the oxygen is released, the resulting deoxyhaemoglobin is darker.

body: When there is an injury to the blood vessels, several actions help prevent excessive blood loss.
Injury to a larger vessel may result in a severe haemorrhage that requires special treatment.
When an arteriole or a venule is cut or broken, the smooth muscles in the wall are stimulated to contract and blood loss lessens almost immediately.

questions.q: A Grade 10 student in Asmara observes a prepared slide of body tissue and sees very narrow vessels whose walls are only one cell thick. Which structural feature of these vessels allows them to carry out the exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between the blood and the tissue fluid?

options.A: They are made of a single layer of simple endothelium, one cell thick
options.B: They are made of three thick, muscular and elastic layers that resist high pressure
options.C: They contain one-way valves along their whole length to prevent backflow
options.D: They have a wide lumen that carries blood away from the heart at high speed

why: **Identify the vessel described.** The vessels described are microscopic and their walls are one cell thick, which is the defining structure of capillaries: microscopic vessels made of a single layer of simple endothelium.

**Recall the function of capillaries.** Capillaries are the only vessels whose thin, semi-permeable walls allow nutrients, respiratory gases and wastes to diffuse between the blood and the surrounding tissue fluid.

**Test each distractor.** Three thick muscular elastic layers describes arteries, not capillaries. One-way valves along the length describe veins, not capillaries. A wide lumen carrying blood away from the heart at high speed again describes an artery, and capillaries do not carry blood away from the heart.
**Conclude.** Only option A correctly states the one-cell-thick simple endothelium, which provides the short diffusion path required for exchange between blood and tissues.

questions.q: Blood leaving the left ventricle is forced into the aorta at high pressure. Which structural feature of arteries is an adaptation to this high pressure?
questions.answer: A. Walls made of thick, muscular and highly elastic tissue in three layers
why: **Recall the function of arteries.** Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so their walls must be able to stretch and recoil without bursting.

**Match structure to function.** Arteries have thick, muscular and highly elastic walls composed of three layers, an adaptation that withstands and smooths the high-pressure surge of each ventricular contraction.

**Eliminate wrong options.** A single layer of simple endothelium describes capillaries; valves at intervals describe veins; a narrow lumen that slows blood before it reaches the tissues contradicts the need for rapid one-way delivery.
**Conclude.** The correct choice is A, the three-layered thick, elastic muscular wall.

questions.q: Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery on its way to the lungs. Which statement best explains why the pulmonary artery is an exception to the usual rule about arteries?

**Apply the rule to the pulmonary artery.** The pulmonary artery arises from the right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs, so it follows the direction rule but breaks the common assumption that arterial blood is oxygenated.
**Check the returning vessel.** Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins, which are veins carrying oxygenated blood.
**Conclude.** Option A is correct: the vessel carries blood away from the heart, but that blood is deoxygenated.

questions.q:
A student in Keren cuts his hand while chopping firewood. The wound bleeds and then stops after a short time. Complete the statements below about the third stage of hemostasis (coagulation) by writing the missing terms.
Injured tissues and platelets release (i) ______. In the presence of calcium ions ($$Ca^{2+}$$) and Vitamin K, (ii) ______ is converted into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then converts the soluble plasma protein (iii) ______ into insoluble (iv) ______ threads that trap blood cells to form a stable clot.
why: **Name the substance released by injured tissue.** During coagulation, injured tissues and platelets release thromboplastin, which starts the clotting cascade, so (i) is thromboplastin.

**Identify the protein activated to thrombin.** In the presence of calcium ions and Vitamin K, thromboplastin brings about the conversion of the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into active thrombin, so (ii) is prothrombin.
**Identify the substrate of thrombin.** Thrombin acts as an enzyme on the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen, converting it into insoluble fibrin, so (iii) is fibrinogen and (iv) is fibrin.
**Interpret the final clot.** The insoluble fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, producing the stable clot that seals the break in the vessel.

**Recall stage 2.** In the platelet plug stage, platelets adhere to exposed collagen fibres of the damaged vessel, change shape and stick together, so the second blank is 'collagen'.
**Check the sequence.** The order is correct: vascular spasm first, platelet plug second, and coagulation third.

why: **Locate the site of clotting-factor production.** Vitamin K is a necessary cofactor for the liver to produce the clotting factor prothrombin, so the first blank is 'liver' and the second is 'prothrombin'.
**Recall why bile is needed.** Vitamin K is fat-soluble and requires bile salts for absorption in the small intestine, so the third blank is 'fat'.

**Link the blockage to the symptom.** A blocked bile duct prevents Vitamin K absorption, the liver therefore makes too little prothrombin, and the clotting cascade fails, producing the easy bruising and bleeding described.

questions.q:
A blood bank in Asmara collects a $$200\text{ mL}$$ sample of whole blood from a donor. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the volume of water contained in that plasma.
(c) Calculate the volume of the sample occupied by the cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets).
questions.answer: (a) $$110\text{ mL}$$ of plasma; (b) $$101.2\text{ mL}$$ of water; (c) $$90\text{ mL}$$ of cellular components
why: **List the given data.** Total blood volume = $$200\text{ mL}$$; plasma = $$55\%$$ of blood volume; water = $$92\%$$ of plasma volume; cellular components = $$45\%$$ of blood volume (since $$100\% - 55\% = 45\%$$).
**Calculate the plasma volume.** Plasma volume = $$55\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.55 \times 200 = 110\text{ mL}$$.
**Calculate the water in the plasma.** Water volume = $$92\%$$ of the plasma volume = $$0.92 \times 110 = 101.2\text{ mL}$$.
**Calculate the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = $$45\%$$ of $$200\text{ mL}$$ = $$0.45 \times 200 = 90\text{ mL}$$.
**Check the result.** The two parts must rebuild the whole sample: $$110\text{ mL} + 90\text{ mL} = 200\text{ mL}$$, which agrees with the given sample volume.

questions.q: During a blood-typing practical at a secondary school in Asmara, the red blood cells of a student are found to carry antigen B and antigen D (Rh), while the plasma contains anti-A antibodies. What is the student's blood group?
why: **Use the antigens to fix the ABO group.** The red cells carry antigen B and the plasma contains anti-A antibodies, which is exactly the pattern of blood group B (B antigen with anti-A antibody).
**Use antigen D to fix the Rh group.** The red cells also carry antigen D, and the presence of antigen D means the blood is Rh-positive; blood lacking antigen D is Rh-negative.

**Test the other options.** Options A and B require antigen A on the red cells, which is absent. Option D requires both A and B antigens and no antibodies in the plasma, but this student has anti-A antibodies.
**Conclude.** The only group matching antigen B, antigen D and anti-A antibodies is B Rh-positive.

questions.q: A patient in Keren is typed before surgery. The red blood cells carry no A antigen and no B antigen and lack antigen D, while the plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies. What is the patient's blood group?
why: **Interpret the absence of A and B antigens.** Red cells with neither A nor B antigen belong to group O, and such plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, exactly as described.
**Interpret the absence of antigen D.** Red cells that lack antigen D are Rh-negative, so the group is O Rh-negative.
**Eliminate the other options.** A Rh-negative carries A antigen; AB Rh-negative carries both A and B antigens and has no antibodies; O Rh-positive would carry antigen D, which is absent here.
**Conclude.** The patient is group O Rh-negative, the universal donor group.

questions.q: An Rh-negative mother has already given birth to one Rh-positive child. During a second pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, the fetus may develop erythroblastosis fetalis because:

why: **Explain how the mother becomes sensitised.** During the first pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, fetal red blood cells enter the Rh-negative mother's blood and stimulate her immune system to produce anti-Rh antibodies.
**Explain the effect in the second pregnancy.** In a later pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus, these already formed anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta and attack the fetal red blood cells.
**Name the outcome.** The destruction of fetal red blood cells produces the condition called erythroblastosis fetalis.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Option B reverses the direction of the antibodies, option C describes clumping of maternal cells rather than destruction of fetal cells, and option D wrongly replaces anti-Rh with anti-A antibodies.

questions.q:
A laboratory technician in Asmara measures the volume of water contained in the plasma of a patient's blood sample and records $$2.53\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume, and plasma is $$92\%$$ water.
(a) Calculate the volume of plasma in the sample.
(b) Calculate the patient's total blood volume.
(c) Calculate the volume occupied by the cellular components.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.75\text{ L}$$ of plasma; (b) $$5.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood; (c) $$2.25\text{ L}$$ of cellular components
why: **Set up the relationships.** Water is $$92\%$$ of plasma, so water $$= 0.92 \times$$ plasma. Plasma is $$55\%$$ of blood, so plasma $$= 0.55 \times$$ blood. The cellular components are the remaining $$45\%$$ of blood.
**Work backwards to the plasma volume.** Since $$0.92 \times \text{plasma} = 2.53\text{ L}$$, the plasma volume is $$\dfrac{2.53}{0.92} = 2.75\text{ L}$$.
**Work backwards to the total blood volume.** Since $$0.55 \times \text{blood} = 2.75\text{ L}$$, the total blood volume is $$\dfrac{2.75}{0.55} = 5.0\text{ L}$$.
**Calculate the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = total blood minus plasma = $$5.0\text{ L} - 2.75\text{ L} = 2.25\text{ L}$$, which also equals $$0.45 \times 5.0 = 2.25\text{ L}$$.
**Check the answer.** Plasma plus cells is $$2.75 + 2.25 = 5.0\text{ L}$$ of blood, and $$92\%$$ of the plasma is $$0.92 \times 2.75 = 2.53\text{ L}$$ of water, matching the measured value.

questions.q: The plasma water in a blood sample taken at a health centre in Asmara is measured as $$2.024\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the plasma volume, the total blood volume and the volume of the cellular components.
questions.answer: $$2.2\text{ L}$$ of plasma, $$4.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood and $$1.8\text{ L}$$ of cellular components
why: **Find the plasma volume.** $$\text{plasma} = \dfrac{2.024}{0.92} = 2.2\text{ L}$$.
**Find the total blood volume.** $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{2.2}{0.55} = 4.0\text{ L}$$.
**Find the cellular volume.** Cellular volume = $$4.0 - 2.2 = 1.8\text{ L}$$, which agrees with $$0.45 \times 4.0 = 1.8\text{ L}$$.
**Check.** $$2.2 + 1.8 = 4.0\text{ L}$$, and $$0.92 \times 2.2 = 2.024\text{ L}$$ of water, as given.

questions.q: The cellular components (red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets) of a patient's blood occupy $$3.6\text{ L}$$. Plasma makes up $$55\%$$ of blood volume and plasma is $$92\%$$ water. Calculate the patient's total blood volume, the plasma volume and the volume of water in that plasma.
questions.answer: $$8.0\text{ L}$$ of total blood, $$4.4\text{ L}$$ of plasma and $$4.048\text{ L}$$ (about $$4.05\text{ L}$$) of water
why: **Use the cellular percentage to find total blood.** Cellular components are $$45\%$$ of blood, so $$\text{blood} = \dfrac{3.6}{0.45} = 8.0\text{ L}$$.
**Find the plasma volume.** $$\text{plasma} = 0.55 \times 8.0 = 4.4\text{ L}$$, which also follows from $$8.0 - 3.6 = 4.4\text{ L}$$.
**Find the water in the plasma.** $$\text{water} = 0.92 \times 4.4 = 4.048\text{ L}$$, approximately $$4.05\text{ L}$$.
**Check.** $$4.4 + 3.6 = 8.0\text{ L}$$, so the plasma and cellular volumes rebuild the total blood volume correctly.

units.title: The Lymphatic System
units.intro:
Capillaries leak fluid into tissues (tissue fluid). Most returns to blood capillaries; the rest becomes **lymph** and is collected by lymph vessels that have valves and pass through **nodes** (filters packed with white cells). Lymph returns to blood near the collarbone veins. Also carries fat from villi (lacteals).

Compared with blood: no red cells, no high-pressure pump — muscles and valves squeeze lymph along. Nodes swell when they are fighting infection.

cards.title: More detail — lymph
body: Tissue fluid is plasma minus most large proteins. At the arterial end of a capillary, pressure pushes fluid out; at the venous end some is sucked back. The leftover is lymph. Vessels start blind-ended, have valves, pass nodes (armpit, neck, groin, mesentery). Spleen and thymus are related lymphoid organs (thymus trains T-cells — Grade 11).
If lymph drainage fails, the limb swells (oedema). After a fatty meal the lymph from the gut looks milky because of lacteals.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Lymph
body: **Lymph** is a colourless fluid containing water, waste materials, cell products (such as hormones and enzymes), digested fat, lymphocytes and phagocytes, which is transported from the blood capillaries by diffusion and filtration.
Rising osmotic pressure of the tissue fluid interferes with osmotic reabsorption of water in the blood capillaries.
The volume and pressure of fluid in the interstitial spaces then tends to increase.
Once tissue fluid enters the lymphatic vessels, it becomes lymph.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Lymphatic Vessels
body: The lymphatic vessels are formed by the lymphatic capillaries, which unite before entering either the thoracic ducts or right lymphatic duct.
The walls of the lymphatic capillaries, like those of the blood capillaries, consist of a single layer of squamous epithelial cells, but are thinner.
The lining of the small intestine contains specialized lymphatic capillaries called lacteals.
The larger lymphatic vessels lead to specialized organs called lymph nodes.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Lymph Nodes
body: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped organs containing large numbers of leukocytes.
Generally, they occur in groups or chains along the paths of the larger lymphatic vessels throughout the body, but are absent in the central nervous system.
Cervical region: nodes in the cervical region occur along the lower border of the mandible, in front of and behind the ears, and deep within the neck along the paths of larger blood vessels.
Axillary region: nodes in the underarm region (armpit) receive lymph from vessels that drain the upper limbs, wall of the thorax, mammary glands (breasts) and upper wall of the abdomen.

cards.title: 3.2 Comparison between the Lymphatic System and the Circulatory System
body: The circulatory and lymphatic systems are two different systems.
The function of the circulatory system is to transport nutrients, oxygen and other useful substances.
The system is also used to remove waste substances, such as carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes produced by cells.
The function of the lymphatic system is to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces.
The substances that leak from the capillaries are collected and returned to the blood circulation by the lymphatic system.

cards.problem: Lymphatic system does not include  A) lymph nodes.  B) spleen.  C) thymus.  D) adrenal glands.  E) lymph vessels.

steps.text: **Step 1.** The lymphatic system includes lymph nodes, lymph vessels, the spleen, and the thymus gland, all of which play roles in immunity. **Adrenal glands** are part of the endocrine system and produce hormones like adrenaline and cortisol; they are not part of the lymphatic system.

glossary.meaning: Lymph is a colourless fluid containing water, waste materials, cell products (such as hormones and enzymes), digested fat, lymphocytes and phagocytes, which is transported from the blood capillaries by diffusion and filtration.
Blood is a fluid tissue that flows in the circulatory system.

tips.text: The lymphatic system is a system consisting of different organs and tissue.
The lymph contains solutes that pass from the blood capillaries. These include ions, nutrients, gases and some proteins; and cell products such as hormones, enzymes and waste products.

The lymphatic system performs the following functions: it helps to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial space, absorbs and transport fat into the blood circulation, and helps in defending the body against diseasecausing agents (as part of the immune system).
The lymph nodes are located at intervals along the lymph and are called lymph glands.
Tonsils form a protective ring of lymphatic tissue around the opening between the nasal and oral cavities. They provide protection against infection in the nose and mouth.
The spleen helps to remove iron from the haemoglobin of the old red blood cells and also produces antibodies against harmful organisms.
The thymus gland plays an important role in the development of the immune response in early life. It is a site of lymphocyte formation and antibody production.
How are nutrients, oxygen and other useful substances transported to all the body’s cells? 2.

questions.q:
Complete the following paragraph using the terms that fit the unit (write the two missing terms in order):

The walls of lymphatic capillaries are made of thin, ____________ endothelial cells that work like one-way swing doors [96, 97]. Because the lymphatic system has no pump of its own [95, 101, 103, 104], lymph is pushed slowly toward the heart by the squeezing action of nearby skeletal muscles, by breathing movements, and by ____________ along all lymphatic vessels that prevent backflow [88, 96, 103, 104].
why: **Recall the wall structure of lymphatic capillaries.** The unit states that lymphatic vessel walls are made of thin, overlapping endothelial cells that act like one-way swing doors: when tissue-fluid pressure outside is high they swing open, and when fluid tries to leave they swing shut, locking the fluid in as lymph [96, 97].

**Recall how lymph is propelled without a pump.** The lymphatic system has no pump [95, 101, 103, 104]. Lymph moves through the massaging action of skeletal muscles, breathing movements, and one-way valves present along all lymphatic vessels, which close if fluid tries to flow backward [88, 96, 103, 104].

**Fill the blanks in order.** First blank: the cells are described as overlapping (not ciliated, not muscular). Second blank: the anti-backflow structures mentioned in the unit are valves. The paragraph therefore reads: overlapping endothelial cells ... and valves along all lymphatic vessels.

**Check the completed sentence.** The completed paragraph now correctly links structure (overlapping endothelial cells producing one-way entry) with mechanism of flow (skeletal muscle squeeze, breathing, and one-way valves), matching the unit exactly [88, 96, 103, 104].

questions.q:
Complete the following paragraph (write the two missing terms in order):

Lymphatic capillaries are microscopic, ____________ capillaries that begin as dead-ends inside the tissues rather than forming a loop [87, 95, 97]. When the pressure of tissue fluid around them rises, fluid pushes the overlapping endothelial cells inward and enters; once inside it becomes ____________, a colourless watery fluid that lacks red blood cells and platelets [87, 95, 103].
why: **Identify the capillary shape.** The unit describes lymphatic capillaries as microscopic, closed-ended capillaries that merge into larger vessels and start as dead-ends in the tissues, unlike the open loops of the circulatory system [87, 95, 97].

**Identify the fluid formed inside.** Once interstitial (tissue) fluid has entered the lymphatic capillary and is locked in by the overlapping cells, it is called lymph: a colourless, watery fluid containing water, leaked proteins, cell products, digested lipids and white blood cells [87, 95].
**Fill the blanks in order.** First blank: closed-ended. Second blank: lymph. The paragraph then reads correctly: lymphatic capillaries are closed-ended ... the fluid becomes lymph.

**Verify against the unit.** Both terms appear in the unit's description of lymph and lymphatic vessels, and the completed sentence keeps the unit's direction of flow (tissue fluid to lymph) intact [87, 95, 96, 97].

**Read the completed paragraph.** The paragraph now reads: intestinal lymphatic capillaries are lacteals, their fatty lymph is chyle, and the spleen filters blood - all directly supported by the unit [86, 94, 97, 100, 102].

questions.q: Large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen sometimes leak from blood capillaries into the tissue spaces. Which statement best explains why these large proteins can enter lymphatic capillaries but cannot re-enter blood capillaries?

options.A: Blood capillaries actively push large proteins back into the blood, but the proteins are too large to be pushed into lymphatic capillaries.
options.B: Blood capillaries have very tiny microscopic pores that block large proteins, while lymphatic capillaries have much larger openings formed by thin, overlapping endothelial cells.
options.C: Large proteins are digested into amino acids in the tissue fluid, absorbed by lymphatic capillaries, and rebuilt as proteins in the blood.
options.D: Large proteins enter lymphatic capillaries only because lymph flows in one direction toward the heart, which pulls them away from blood capillaries.

why: **State what limits exchange at blood capillaries.** Blood capillaries have thin walls with very tiny microscopic pores. These pores allow water and small solutes to pass in two-way exchange but are too small for large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, so once leaked these proteins cannot diffuse back into the blood [85, 93, 66, 74, 75].

**State the structural feature of lymphatic capillaries.** Lymphatic capillaries are built from thin, overlapping endothelial cells that form large, flap-like openings. When tissue-fluid pressure rises these flaps swing inward and open, so even large proteins can enter the lymphatic capillary [95, 96, 97].

**Link the two facts to the question.** The deciding factor is the size of the openings: tiny pores in blood capillaries exclude large proteins, whereas the large overlapping-cell openings of lymphatic capillaries admit them. This is why the lymphatic system is essential for returning leaked proteins to the blood and preventing loss of osmotic pressure and severe edema [85, 93, 95].

**Test every option.** A is false: the unit gives no active transport of proteins back into blood, and it states the opposite about lymphatic entry. C is false: lymph contains dissolved proteins that leaked from blood capillaries; there is no digestion-and-rebuilding step in the unit. D is false: one-way lymph flow explains direction of movement, not why a large molecule is able to pass through a wall. Only B states the true structural reason.

**Conclude.** Option B is the only statement supported by the unit, because it correctly contrasts the tiny pores of blood capillaries with the large openings of lymphatic capillaries [85, 93, 95, 96].
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A patient suffering from severe protein deficiency produces too few plasma proteins, so tissue fluid is not drawn back into the blood capillaries efficiently. Which statement best explains why the resulting accumulation of tissue fluid is called edema?
questions.answer: D. Edema is the swelling caused by excess fluid accumulating in the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system normally drains this fluid back to the bloodstream.
why: **Define the starting problem.** Some plasma proteins leak out of blood capillaries and are needed to maintain osmotic pressure; when proteins are lost or scarce, water is not reabsorbed well and collects in the interstitial spaces [75, 85, 93, 95].

**Recall what edema is.** The unit defines edema (swelling) as the flooding that results when leaked tissue fluid is allowed to accumulate in the interstitial spaces instead of being drained away [95].

**Recall the drainage route.** The lymphatic capillaries and vessels collect the excess fluid and large leaked proteins and return them to the venous bloodstream near the heart [85, 93, 95]. If this drainage fails or is overwhelmed, fluid stays in the tissues and swelling appears [95].

**Test every option.** A is false: edema is not a shortage of red blood cells. B is false: edema is not caused by rapid movement of lymph into arteries; lymph enters veins near the heart. C is false: swelling is not the trapping of pathogens inside the blood only. D correctly defines edema as interstitial fluid accumulation normally drained by the lymphatic system.
**Conclude.** Option D is the single defensible answer because it matches the unit's cause (untrained tissue fluid) and the lymphatic system's drainage role [85, 93, 95].

questions.q: Blood is a red, viscous tissue that contains red blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins, whereas lymph is a clear or milky fluid. Which statement best describes the cellular content of healthy lymph?
questions.answer: A. Lymph contains white blood cells (phagocytes and lymphocytes) but completely lacks red blood cells and platelets.
why: **Recall the composition of lymph.** The unit describes lymph as a colourless, watery fluid containing water, dissolved leaked proteins, cell products such as hormones and enzymes, digested lipids, and white blood cells - especially lymphocytes and phagocytes [87, 95].
**Recall the composition of blood.** Blood is a red, viscous tissue containing red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen [66, 74, 75].

**Compare the two fluids.** Subtracting the blood list from the lymph list leaves white blood cells present in lymph but red blood cells and platelets completely absent. This is one of the unit's listed differences in fluid composition [87, 95, 103].

**Test every option.** B is false: red blood cells and platelets are absent, not abundant. C is false: platelets are absent from lymph. D is false: large plasma proteins are not the cellular component of lymph, and lymph does contain white blood cells.
**Conclude.** Option A is the only statement consistent with the unit: lymph carries white blood cells only, with no red blood cells and no platelets [87, 95, 103].

questions.q: A patient recovering from a leg injury lies still for 3 hours. Because there is no walking movement to squeeze the lymphatic vessels, excess tissue fluid collects in the leg at a steady rate of $$180\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. A nurse then performs a 20-minute manual lymphatic drainage massage that removes $$75\%$$ of the fluid collected. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces after the massage.
questions.answer: $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.
why: **Identify the principle.** When skeletal muscles do not contract, the massaging action that normally pushes lymph along is lost, so tissue fluid collects in the interstitial spaces [88, 96, 104]. The volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid collected in 3 hours.** Collected fluid $$= 180\ \text{mL/hour} \times 3\ \text{hours} = 540\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the volume removed by the massage.** Removed fluid $$= 75\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL} = 0.75 \times 540 = 405\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 540\ \text{mL} - 405\ \text{mL} = 135\ \text{mL}$$, which is the same as $$25\%$$ of $$540\ \text{mL}$$.

**State the result.** After the massage, $$135\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still left in the leg tissues, so the drainage has only partly corrected the accumulation. This remaining fluid is what would be seen as pitting swelling (edema) until normal muscle movement resumes [88, 95, 96, 104].

questions.q: During a long bus journey from Asmara to Massawa, a passenger sits without moving for 4 hours and interstitial fluid accumulates in the ankles at a steady rate of $$160\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. After the journey, 85% of this accumulated fluid is drained away as the passenger walks and the calf muscles squeeze the lymphatic vessels. Calculate the volume of fluid, in millilitres, remaining in the ankle tissues.
questions.answer: $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid remains in the ankle tissues.
why: **Identify the principle.** Lymph has no pump, so prolonged sitting without skeletal muscle contraction allows tissue fluid to collect in the lower limbs, and only muscle movement restores drainage [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid accumulated.** Accumulated fluid $$= 160\ \text{mL/hour} \times 4\ \text{hours} = 640\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the fluid drained.** Drained fluid $$= 85\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL} = 0.85 \times 640 = 544\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 640\ \text{mL} - 544\ \text{mL} = 96\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$15\%$$ of $$640\ \text{mL}$$.
**State the result.** About $$96\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid is still trapped in the ankle tissues after walking, which is why ankles can stay puffy for a while after a long sedentary journey [71, 95, 96].

questions.q: A nurse uses a compression bandage on a patient whose foot is swollen after an infection. Over 2.5 hours, tissue fluid collects in the foot at a steady rate of $$200\ \text{mL/hour}$$ [88, 96, 104]. The bandage and gentle elevation then drain away $$72\%$$ of the collected fluid. Calculate the volume of lymph, in millilitres, still left in the tissue spaces.
questions.answer: $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of lymph remains in the tissue spaces.
why: **Identify the principle.** With impaired lymph movement, interstitial fluid accumulates and can be partly removed by external compression together with the muscle and breathing movements that normally drive lymph toward the heart [88, 96, 104]. Volume collected equals rate multiplied by time.
**Calculate the fluid collected.** Collected fluid $$= 200\ \text{mL/hour} \times 2.5\ \text{hours} = 500\ \text{mL}$$ [88, 96].
**Calculate the fluid drained.** Drained fluid $$= 72\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL} = 0.72 \times 500 = 360\ \text{mL}$$.
**Calculate the fluid remaining.** Remaining fluid $$= 500\ \text{mL} - 360\ \text{mL} = 140\ \text{mL}$$, which equals $$28\%$$ of $$500\ \text{mL}$$.
**State the result.** The bandage leaves $$140\ \text{mL}$$ of fluid in the foot tissues, so drainage is incomplete and the swelling only partly subsides [95, 96, 104].

questions.q:
The heart of a healthy adult at rest pumps $$7500\ \text{mL}$$ of blood every minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$2.4\%$$ leaks out of the blood capillaries into the interstitial spaces as tissue fluid, and $$92\%$$ of that leaked fluid is eventually collected and returned to the bloodstream by the lymphatic system [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the total volume of lymph returned to the bloodstream in one day, giving your answer in litres.
(b) The same adult's spleen destroys old, damaged red blood cells at a rate that releases $$30\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and this iron is sent to the red bone marrow for recycling. If each newly manufactured red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], calculate the number of new red blood cells that can be produced in 30 days from the recycled iron.
questions.answer: (a) $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$238.5\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 30 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 2.4\%$$ of $$7500\ \text{mL/min} = 0.024 \times 7500 = 180\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 92\%$$ of $$180\ \text{mL/min} = 0.92 \times 180 = 165.6\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].

**Convert the rate to litres per day.** In one day (24 hours $$= 1440$$ minutes) the volume is $$165.6\ \text{mL/min} \times 1440\ \text{min} = 238464\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$, this is $$238.464\ \text{L} \approx 238\ \text{L/day}$$ (about $$238.5\ \text{L}$$).
**Find the iron salvaged in 30 days.** Iron per day $$= 30\ \text{mg} = 0.030\ \text{g}$$, so in 30 days the spleen releases $$30 \times 0.030\ \text{g} = 0.90\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of new red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.90\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells. This is the iron recycled to the red bone marrow to manufacture new haemoglobin for developing red blood cells [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** Part (a): roughly 238 litres of lymph per day means the lymphatic system returns a volume comparable to the whole blood plasma volume many times over each day, consistent with continuous capillary leakage [85, 93, 95]. Part (b): $$4.5 \times 10^{11}$$ cells in 30 days (about $$1.5 \times 10^{10}$$ cells per day) is a large but plausible replacement rate for a marrow continuously recycling iron from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100].

questions.q:
During hard farm work in the Keren area, a man's heart pumps $$9000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.0\%$$ leaks into the interstitial spaces, and the lymphatic system returns $$95\%$$ of the leaked fluid to the bloodstream [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned per day, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$25\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day from destroyed red blood cells [77, 100]. If each new red blood cell needs $$2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77], how many new red blood cells can his marrow produce in 40 days from this recycled iron?
questions.answer: (a) $$369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day (accept $$369.4\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 40 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.0\%$$ of $$9000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.030 \times 9000 = 270\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 95\%$$ of $$270\ \text{mL/min} = 0.95 \times 270 = 256.5\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].
**Convert to litres per day.** In 1440 minutes the volume is $$256.5 \times 1440 = 369360\ \text{mL} = 369.36\ \text{L} \approx 369\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per day.
**Find the iron salvaged in 40 days.** Iron per day $$= 25\ \text{mg} = 0.025\ \text{g}$$; in 40 days the spleen releases $$40 \times 0.025\ \text{g} = 1.0\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{1.0\ \text{g}}{2.5 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, all built from recycled iron sent to the red bone marrow [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** Heavier exercise increases cardiac output and capillary leakage, so both the leak (270 mL/min) and the returned lymph (about 369 L/day) are larger than in the resting adult, as expected [61, 69, 85, 93]. Part (b) gives $$4.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 40 days, a plausible marrow replacement rate [77, 100].

questions.q:
A Massawa fish-processor works in hot conditions and his heart pumps $$8000\ \text{mL}$$ of blood per minute [48, 57, 61, 69]. Of this, $$3.5\%$$ becomes tissue fluid and the lymphatic system drains $$90\%$$ of it back into the blood [85, 93, 95, 104].

(a) Calculate the volume of lymph returned in one hour, in litres.
(b) His spleen releases $$40\ \text{mg}$$ of iron per day [77, 100], and each new red blood cell needs $$2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77]. How many new red blood cells can be made from the iron salvaged in 15 days?
questions.answer: (a) $$15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour (accept $$15.1\ \text{L}$$). (b) $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ new red blood cells in 15 days.
why: **Find the fluid leaking per minute.** Leaked tissue fluid $$= 3.5\%$$ of $$8000\ \text{mL/min} = 0.035 \times 8000 = 280\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95].
**Find the lymph returned per minute.** Lymph returned $$= 90\%$$ of $$280\ \text{mL/min} = 0.90 \times 280 = 252\ \text{mL/min}$$ [85, 93, 95, 104].
**Convert to litres per hour.** In 60 minutes the volume is $$252 \times 60 = 15120\ \text{mL} = 15.12\ \text{L} \approx 15\ \text{L}$$ of lymph per hour.
**Find the iron salvaged in 15 days.** Iron per day $$= 40\ \text{mg} = 0.040\ \text{g}$$; in 15 days the spleen releases $$15 \times 0.040\ \text{g} = 0.60\ \text{g}$$ of iron [77, 100].

**Find the number of red blood cells.** Number of cells $$= \dfrac{0.60\ \text{g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{g per cell}} = 3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells, produced in the red bone marrow from recycled iron [77].

**Check the answers for sense.** The hourly figure $$15.12\ \text{L/hour}$$ equals about $$363\ \text{L/day}$$, in the same order of magnitude as the resting case after allowing for the larger leak and slightly lower drainage fraction; $$3.0 \times 10^{11}$$ cells over 15 days is consistent with the daily iron release [77, 85, 93, 100].
