questions.q:
The thymus gland is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum [100]. It is relatively large in infants but gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

(a) Explain the biological reason why the thymus is large and active in an infant and why it shrinks after puberty [100].
(b) In a particular Eritrean child, the thymus weighs $$44\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and then involutes at a steady rate of $$0.9\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 10 years of involution, and then calculate the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, so it is large and active early in life; once the immune system is fully developed and stocked with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty) its active role declines and it involutes, shrinking as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100]. (b) Mass after 10 years $$= 35\ \text{g}$$, and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass is $$\dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 \approx 20.5\%$$.
why: **State the role of the thymus early in life.** The unit states that the thymus plays an essential role early in life as the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses [100]. It is therefore most active while the immune system is being built up in infancy and childhood.

**Explain the shrinking after puberty.** Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, typically around puberty, the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution, gradually shrinking and being replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].
**Calculate the mass lost over 10 years.** Mass lost $$= 0.9\ \text{g/year} \times 10\ \text{years} = 9\ \text{g}$$ [100].
**Calculate the mass after 10 years.** Mass after involution $$= 44\ \text{g} - 9\ \text{g} = 35\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{\text{mass lost}}{\text{puberty mass}} \times 100 = \dfrac{9}{44} \times 100 = 20.45\% \approx 20.5\%$$.

**State the final result.** After 10 years the thymus weighs $$35\ \text{g}$$, a decrease of about $$20.5\%$$ from its $$44\ \text{g}$$ mass at puberty, matching the unit's statement that the gland shrinks after puberty as it is replaced by fat and connective tissue [100].

questions.q:
(a) Explain why a person who had their thymus removed as a young adult might still fight infections reasonably well, even though the gland has a vital early role [100].
(b) In another child the thymus weighs $$40\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes at a steady rate of $$0.8\ \text{g}$$ per year [100]. Calculate its mass after 20 years and the percentage decrease from its puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus's essential role is early in life, where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop; by adulthood the immune system is already fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells, so much of its protective capacity persists even after the gland involutes or is removed [100]. (b) Mass after 20 years $$= 24\ \text{g}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.
why: **Recall the thymus's early role.** The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and immune responses develop, which is why it is essential early in life and relatively large in infants [100].

**Explain why protection persists later.** Once the immune system is fully developed and populated with long-lived memory T-cells (around puberty), the thymus's active role decreases and it undergoes involution [100]. The mature, long-lived lymphocytes already produced continue to provide immune protection, so infections can still be fought reasonably well after the gland is lost.
**Calculate the mass lost over 20 years.** Mass lost $$= 0.8\ \text{g/year} \times 20\ \text{years} = 16\ \text{g}$$ [100].
**Calculate the mass after 20 years.** Mass after involution $$= 40\ \text{g} - 16\ \text{g} = 24\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40\%$$.
**State the final result.** The thymus falls from $$40\ \text{g}$$ to $$24\ \text{g}$$, a $$40\%$$ decrease, illustrating the progressive involution described in the unit [100].

questions.q:
(a) Explain how the thymus differs in function from the spleen, even though both are lymphatic organs [100, 102].
(b) A patient's thymus weighs $$36\ \text{g}$$ at puberty and involutes steadily to $$21\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100]. Calculate the yearly rate of mass loss in grams per year and the percentage decrease from the puberty mass.
questions.answer: (a) The thymus is the site where T-lymphocytes mature and develop immune responses early in life [100], whereas the spleen is a blood filter that removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood [100, 102]. (b) Rate of loss $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$; percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 \approx 41.7\%$$.
why: **State the thymus's function.** The thymus is a triangular, bilobed gland behind the sternum that serves as the maturation site for T-lymphocytes early in life and gradually shrinks after puberty [100].

**State the spleen's function.** The spleen, the largest lymphatic organ in the upper left abdomen, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old damaged red blood cells, recycles iron from haemoglobin, produces antibodies and stores extra blood for release during heavy bleeding [100, 102].
**Calculate the mass lost.** Mass lost $$= 36\ \text{g} - 21\ \text{g} = 15\ \text{g}$$ over 12 years [100].
**Calculate the yearly rate of loss.** Rate $$= \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{12\ \text{years}} = 1.25\ \text{g/year}$$.
**Calculate the percentage decrease.** Percentage decrease $$= \dfrac{15}{36} \times 100 = 41.67\% \approx 41.7\%$$.
**State the final result.** The thymus loses $$1.25\ \text{g}$$ each year, a $$41.7\%$$ decrease from its $$36\ \text{g}$$ puberty mass, consistent with the unit's account of involution [100].

units.title: The Immune System
units.intro:
**Antigen** = foreign marker. **Antibody** = protein shaped to stick to that marker. White cells: some eat pathogens (phagocytes), some remember and make antibodies (lymphocytes).

**Active immunity:** your body meets the antigen (infection or vaccine) and makes its own memory. Lasts. **Passive:** you borrow ready antibodies (breast milk, injection). Fast but short.

cards.title: 4.1 Antigens and Antibodies
body: Anything that can trigger an immune response in the body is called an **antigen**.
An antigen can be a whole microbe (bacteria or a small parasite, such as a virus) or even a part of a microbe.
Tissue or cells from a donor (apart from an identical twin) can also act as antigens if given to a recipient.
In the recipient’s body, this tissue is capable of triggering an immune response, because it is foreign to the recipient.
Antibodies are protein substances produced by white blood cells in response to antigens.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Active Immunity
body: Natural acquired active immunity: This type of immunity is produced when a disease-causing agent is introduced into the body by natural means (non-intentional).
For example when an individual is infected, the body produces specific antibodies against the disease-causing antigens or their products.
The antibodies continue to form after recovery, resulting in permanent active immunity.
Diphtheria, measles and mumps are diseases that often trigger this kind of immune response.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Passive Immunity
body: Natural acquired passive immunity: This is immunity that is acquired naturally when an unborn infant receives antibodies from its mother through the placenta or in the first breast-milk received from the already immune mother.
Artificial acquired passive immunity: This is an immunity that is acquired when an individual receives antibodies produced in another individual (human to human) or animal (animal to human).
The introduction of serum that contains ready-made antibodies is important for individuals who cannot fight a disease and produce their own antibodies.
In most cases, this type of immunity lasts from a few weeks to several months.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the terms active vs. passive and natural vs. artificial**
* **Active**: The body is exposed to antigens and produces its own antibodies.

glossary.meaning: Immunity is a term that describes the state of having sufficient defences to avoid infection, disease or other unwanted invasion.
Immunity in which the body makes its own antibodies, after an infection or a vaccine; it is long-lasting.
Immunity from ready-made antibodies received from outside (from the mother or by injection); it is immediate but short-lived.

tips.text: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist infection from exposure to a micro-organism or parasite.

Before any foreign particle establishes itself inside the body of an animal, it has to bypass the physical components of the immune system, such as the skin and mucus, and resist chemical defences (tears, mucus secretions and saliva).
Once the foreign particle gets through the physical barriers, the advanced components of the immune system become active and generate specific antibodies.
Antibodies are proteins produced by white blood cells to specifically fight foreign substances known as antigens.
Antigens are macromolecules that induce certain responses in the immune system.

Immunity is the ability of the body to resist an infectious disease. These can be broadly classified as specific or non-specific components. This type of immunity is called innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

The other components of the immune system, adapt themselves to each new disease encountered and are able to generate a specific type of immunity for a specific pathogen or antigen during the lifetime of an individual.
The components of the immune system are grouped in a type of immunity called acquired immunity.

Inborn immunity refers to a phenomenon in which genetic characteristics common to a particular kind of organism or species provide defences against certain pathogens. Such individuals or species are said to have natural immunity.
For example the immunity of the body against many animal diseases (such as hog cholera, cattle plague, and distemper) and the natural immunity of some individuals to tuberculosis.

questions.q: The trachea and bronchi are lined with a mucous membrane that contains sticky mucus and fine, beating cilia. Which statement correctly describes what happens to bacteria that become trapped in this mucus?

options.A: They are swept downwards by the cilia into the lungs, where they are engulfed by phagocytes in the alveoli.
options.B: They are swept upwards by the cilia to the pharynx, swallowed, and destroyed by the acidic gastric juice in the stomach.
options.C: They are killed exactly where they are trapped by keratin secreted by the ciliated epithelial cells.
options.D: They are dissolved by the fatty acids present in the mucus and then absorbed into the blood.

why: **Identify the defence structure.** The trachea and bronchi are lined by the mucociliary escalator, which is part of the non-specific first line of defence and consists of sticky mucus plus fine, beating cilia.
**Trapping of the microbes.** Inhaled bacteria, dust and spores stick to the mucus secreted by the mucous membrane of the air passages.
**Direction of the ciliary beat.** The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the microbe-laden mucus upwards towards the pharynx; they do not beat downwards into the lungs.
**Chemical destruction in the stomach.** The mucus is swallowed, and the trapped microbes are instantly digested by the highly acidic gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$).

**Test the distractors.** Keratin is a protein of the cornified skin layer, not a secretion of ciliated cells, so C is wrong; fatty acids occur in sweat and sebum on the skin, not in airway mucus, so D is wrong; and because the cilia beat upwards, A is wrong. Only B matches the mucociliary escalator.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A child in Asmara inhales dust carrying bacteria. The bacteria are trapped in the sticky mucus of the air passages. In which organ are these trapped microorganisms finally destroyed by hydrochloric acid?
why: **Trapping in the airways.** The nasal passages, trachea and bronchi are lined with sticky mucus that traps inhaled bacteria and dust.
**Upward transport.** The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the dust-laden mucus upwards to the pharynx.
**Swallowing and acid digestion.** The mucus is swallowed into the stomach, where gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$) instantly digests the microorganisms.

**Reject the other options.** The alveoli are below the trachea and the cilia beat upwards, so A is wrong; the lymph nodes and bone marrow are sites where antibodies are manufactured, not sites of acid destruction, so C and D are wrong.

questions.q: Explain the role of the cilia that line the trachea, and state what would happen to the trapped dust and bacteria if these cilia stopped beating.
questions.answer: The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the sticky mucus, together with the dust and bacteria trapped in it, upwards to the pharynx so that it can be swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid. If the cilia stopped beating, the mucus would no longer be swept upwards: it would accumulate in the air passages and the trapped microorganisms could remain in the respiratory tract and cause infection.
why: **Describe the lining.** The trachea is lined with a mucous membrane that contains goblet cells secreting sticky mucus and ciliated epithelial cells.
**State the normal role of cilia.** The cilia beat rhythmically and move the mucus with its trapped microbes upwards to the pharynx, where it is swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid.

**Predict the consequence of ciliary failure.** Without the ciliary beat the mucus is not transported, so it accumulates and the trapped bacteria and dust stay in the respiratory tract, raising the risk of infection.

questions.q: Complete the following statement: Antigens are macromolecules that are recognised as foreign by the body and trigger an immune response; on the surface of microbes they are usually ______ or ______.
why: **Recall what an antigen is.** An antigen is any macromolecule that is recognised as foreign by the body and triggers an immune response.
**Recall the chemical nature of antigens.** The unit states that antigens are usually proteins or polysaccharides located on the surface of microbes.
**Complete the statement.** The two missing words are proteins and polysaccharides.

questions.q:
A baby girl is born in a health centre in Asmara. Before birth she received maternal antibodies across the placenta, and after birth she received more through colostrum. This natural passive immunity protects her for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days.
(a) For how many days does the maternal antibody protection last?
(b) At the age of $$5$$ months she is given the measles vaccine. Her own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce enough antibodies and memory cells. Is there any period during which she is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) Name the type of acquired immunity she has once her own antibodies have been produced, and state whether memory cells are present.
questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: her own antibodies appear on day $$160$$ while maternal protection lasts until day $$180$$, giving an overlap of $$20$$ days. (c) Artificial active immunity, with memory cells present.
why: **Classify the immunity from the mother.** Antibodies crossing the placenta and passing in colostrum are ready-made antibodies produced by the mother, so the baby has natural passive immunity; her own cells made none of these antibodies.
**Calculate the duration of maternal protection.** The protection lasts $$6$$ months, and $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days, so the duration is $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days.
**Find the day the vaccine is given.** At $$5$$ months of age she is $$5 \times 30 = 150$$ days old when the vaccine is given.
**Find when her own antibodies appear.** Her B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days after vaccination, so her own protective antibodies appear on day $$150 + 10 = 160$$.

**Check for a gap in protection.** Maternal antibodies protect her until day $$180$$, and her own antibodies begin on day $$160$$. Since $$160 < 180$$, there is no unprotected period; the two protections overlap for $$180 - 160 = 20$$ days.

**Classify the vaccine-induced immunity.** The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the girl's own B-lymphocytes to make antibodies, so she develops artificial active immunity, and memory B-cells are formed.
**State the conclusions.** (a) $$180$$ days of maternal protection; (b) no gap, with a $$20$$-day overlap; (c) artificial active immunity, and memory cells are present.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A newborn boy in Keren receives maternal antibodies that give him natural passive immunity for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days. He is given the BCG vaccine at the age of $$4$$ months, and his body needs $$14$$ days to build up protective antibody levels.
(a) How many days does the maternal protection last?
(b) Is there any period during which he is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning and state the number of overlapping days.
questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$134$$ and maternal protection continues until day $$180$$, so there are $$46$$ days of overlap.
why: **Duration of maternal protection.** $$6$$ months at $$30$$ days each gives $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days of natural passive immunity.
**Day of vaccination.** At $$4$$ months of age the boy is $$4 \times 30 = 120$$ days old.
**Day his own antibodies appear.** His body needs $$14$$ days after vaccination, so his own antibodies appear on day $$120 + 14 = 134$$.
**Compare the two dates.** Since day $$134$$ is earlier than day $$180$$, the boy is never unprotected; the protections overlap for $$180 - 134 = 46$$ days.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A man in Massawa is injected with anti-tetanus serum after a deep wound, and at the same time he begins a course of tetanus vaccine. The injected serum provides ready-made antibodies that protect him for $$21$$ days, while his own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce protective antibodies.
(a) Name the type of immunity given by the serum and the type that the vaccine will produce.
(b) Is there any period during which he is unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) For how many days do the injected antibodies and his own antibodies overlap?
questions.answer: (a) The serum gives artificial passive immunity; the vaccine produces artificial active immunity. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$10$$ while the injected antibodies last until day $$21$$. (c) $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days of overlap.
why: **Classify the serum injection.** Ready-made antibodies produced by another human or animal and injected into the patient give artificial passive immunity, which acts immediately but forms no memory cells.
**Classify the vaccination course.** The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the patient's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity with memory cells.
**Compare the two time courses.** The injected antibodies protect from day $$0$$ to day $$21$$, and his own antibodies begin on day $$10$$.
**Decide whether a gap exists.** Because day $$10$$ comes before day $$21$$, protection is continuous; the overlap is $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A boy in Massawa is bitten by a stray dog suspected of carrying rabies. The doctor immediately injects him with anti-rabies serum and also begins a course of rabies vaccine. Using the types of acquired immunity:
(a) Name the type of acquired immunity provided by the serum injection.
(b) Name the type of acquired immunity that the vaccine course will produce.
(c) Explain why the serum is given immediately but the vaccine cannot protect the boy during the first few days.
(d) State which of the two provides immunological memory.
questions.answer: (a) Artificial passive immunity. (b) Artificial active immunity. (c) The serum already contains ready-made antibodies that bind and neutralise the rabies virus immediately, whereas active immunity takes several days because the boy's own B-lymphocytes must first produce the antibodies. (d) Only the vaccine course, that is artificial active immunity, provides memory cells.
why: **Classify the serum injection.** The serum contains ready-made antibodies produced by another immune human or animal, so it gives artificial passive immunity.
**Classify the vaccine course.** The vaccine contains dead, weakened or fragmented pathogens (antigens) that stimulate the boy's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity.

**Compare the speeds of protection.** Passive immunity is immediate because the injected antibodies can bind and neutralise the rabies virus at once; active immunity is slow because the body must first detect the antigen and its B-lymphocytes must divide, differentiate into plasma cells and synthesise new antibodies, which takes several days.

**Apply this to the emergency.** Rabies is highly dangerous, so the boy cannot wait several days for his own active response; the ready-made serum neutralises the virus immediately while the vaccine builds long-term protection in the background.

**Decide where memory comes from.** Only the vaccine (artificial active immunity) stimulates the boy's own cells, so only it forms memory B-cells; the injected serum provides no immunological memory and its antibodies are eventually broken down.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A girl in Keren becomes ill with mumps, recovers fully, and is never infected again.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does she now have?
(b) Would she still need a mumps vaccine later? Explain your answer using the idea of memory cells.
questions.answer: (a) Natural active immunity. (b) No: she already has memory B-cells from the natural infection, and these recognise the mumps pathogen instantly on a second exposure and produce antibodies rapidly, so vaccination is unnecessary.
why: **Identify how the immunity was acquired.** She caught mumps naturally and her own immune system fought the infection, so the immunity is natural active immunity.
**Explain the lasting protection.** During the natural infection her B-lymphocytes produced antibodies and left long-lived memory cells, so protection is long-lasting.
**Answer the vaccine question.** Because memory cells respond immediately if the same pathogen returns, re-infection is prevented and an additional vaccine is not needed.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A newborn baby in Nakfa is fed colostrum, the first breast milk, which is rich in maternal antibodies.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does the baby receive?
(b) Why does this protection last only about the first $$6$$ months and not a lifetime?
(c) Does the baby form memory cells against the pathogens covered by these antibodies? Explain.
questions.answer: (a) Natural passive immunity. (b) The antibodies are ready-made and were not produced by the baby's own cells, so they are gradually broken down and the protection lasts only a few months (about $$6$$ months in this case). (c) No: because the baby's own B-lymphocytes were never stimulated, no memory cells are formed.
why: **Classify the transferred antibodies.** Antibodies passed from mother to offspring through the placenta or through colostrum give natural passive immunity.

**Explain the short duration.** The baby did not manufacture these antibodies, so they are eventually broken down and the protection lasts only a short time, protecting the infant for about the first $$6$$ months of life.
**Explain the lack of memory.** Since the baby's own B-lymphocytes were not stimulated by the antigens, no memory cells are produced.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
During a measles outbreak in a district near Nakfa, health workers study $$4000$$ children. $$3200$$ of the children had previously received the measles vaccine and $$800$$ had never been vaccinated. During the outbreak, $$8\%$$ of the unvaccinated children and $$0.25\%$$ of the vaccinated children contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of children who contracted measles in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of measles cases among the $$4000$$ children.
(c) What percentage of all the measles cases came from the unvaccinated group? Give your answer to one decimal place.
(d) State the type of acquired immunity that the vaccinated children were expected to have, and explain, in terms of memory cells, why so few of them became ill.
questions.answer: (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated children and $$8$$ vaccinated children. (b) $$72$$ measles cases in total. (c) $$88.9\%$$ of the cases came from the unvaccinated group. (d) The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity; the vaccine antigens made their B-lymphocytes form memory cells, which recognise the measles pathogen quickly on re-exposure and produce antibodies before the disease develops.
why: **List the group sizes.** There are $$800$$ unvaccinated children and $$3200$$ vaccinated children, giving a total of $$4000$$ children studied.
**Cases among the unvaccinated children.** $$8\%$$ of $$800$$ means $$800 \times \frac{8}{100} = 64$$ children contracted measles.
**Cases among the vaccinated children.** $$0.25\%$$ of $$3200$$ means $$3200 \times \frac{0.25}{100} = 3200 \times 0.0025 = 8$$ children contracted measles.
**Total cases in the district.** Adding the two groups gives $$64 + 8 = 72$$ measles cases in total.
**Percentage of cases from the unvaccinated group.** The unvaccinated group contributed $$64$$ of the $$72$$ cases, so the percentage is $$\frac{64}{72} \times 100 = 88.888... \approx 88.9\%$$.

**Explain the difference using immunity.** The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity: the vaccine antigens stimulated their B-lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells, so on re-exposure to measles the memory cells recognised the pathogen at once and produced antibodies rapidly, preventing the disease from developing.
**State the final answers.** (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated and $$8$$ vaccinated children; (b) $$72$$ cases; (c) $$88.9\%$$; (d) artificial active immunity supported by memory cells.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
An oral polio immunization campaign in Asmara covers $$5000$$ children: $$4500$$ children receive the vaccine and $$500$$ remain unvaccinated. In a later outbreak, $$6\%$$ of the unvaccinated children and $$0.2\%$$ of the vaccinated children are infected.
(a) Calculate the number of infected children in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of infections.
(c) What percentage of all the infections came from the vaccinated group? Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) $$30$$ unvaccinated children and $$9$$ vaccinated children. (b) $$39$$ infections in total. (c) $$\frac{9}{39} \times 100 = 23.1\%$$ came from the vaccinated group.
why: **List the group sizes.** There are $$500$$ unvaccinated children and $$4500$$ vaccinated children, giving $$5000$$ children in total.
**Infections among the unvaccinated children.** $$6\%$$ of $$500$$ equals $$500 \times \frac{6}{100} = 30$$ infected children.
**Infections among the vaccinated children.** $$0.2\%$$ of $$4500$$ equals $$4500 \times \frac{0.2}{100} = 4500 \times 0.002 = 9$$ infected children.
**Total infections.** $$30 + 9 = 39$$ infections in total.
**Percentage from the vaccinated group.** The vaccinated group contributed $$9$$ of the $$39$$ infections, so the percentage is $$\frac{9}{39} \times 100 = 23.076... \approx 23.1\%$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A health centre in Keren reports that of $$2500$$ children who received the measles vaccine, $$0.4\%$$ later contracted measles, while of the $$500$$ children who were not vaccinated, $$15\%$$ contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of cases in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of cases.
(c) How many times greater was the infection rate among the unvaccinated children than among the vaccinated children?
questions.answer: (a) $$10$$ vaccinated children and $$75$$ unvaccinated children contracted measles. (b) $$85$$ cases in total. (c) The infection rate was $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater among the unvaccinated children.
why: **Cases among the vaccinated children.** $$0.4\%$$ of $$2500$$ equals $$2500 \times \frac{0.4}{100} = 2500 \times 0.004 = 10$$ children.
**Cases among the unvaccinated children.** $$15\%$$ of $$500$$ equals $$500 \times \frac{15}{100} = 75$$ children.
**Total number of cases.** $$10 + 75 = 85$$ cases in total.
**Compare the two infection rates.** The rate in the unvaccinated group was $$15\%$$ and in the vaccinated group $$0.4\%$$, so the ratio is $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater.

**Relate the rates to immunity.** The vaccinated children had artificial active immunity with memory B-cells, which explains the far lower infection rate; the unvaccinated children depended only on non-specific defences and, if infected, on slow natural active immunity.

units.title: The Respiratory System
units.intro:
Nose (warm, filter, moisten) → pharynx → trachea (rings of cartilage) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (huge surface, thin, moist, capillary wrap).

**Inhale:** diaphragm down, ribs up and out → chest volume up → pressure down → air in. **Exhale:** opposite (often passive at rest).

cards.title: 5.1.1 The Nose
body: The human respiratory system starts with the nose.
The nose encloses the nasal cavity, which opens to the outside through openings called the nostrils.
The air that enters the body through the nose is warmed, filtered and moistened as it passes through the nasal cavity.
Fine hairs (cilia) lining the cavity filter the inhaled air before it passes down the pharynx.

cards.title: 5.1.2 The Pharynx
body: **The pharynx** is a tube-like structure, and is a part of both the respiratory and digestive systems.
Air is breathed in through the trachea into the lungs, whereas food passes down the oesophagus to the stomach.
The pharynx extends into a slit or narrow opening, known as glottis, which leads into the larynx.
The opening is guarded by a flap of tissue called the epiglottis.

cards.title: 5.1.3 The Trachea
body: The trachea extends from the neck to the thorax, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi (singular: bronchus).
The two main bronchi enter the right and left lungs.
Inside the lung, each bronchus branches into several bronchioles.
A single layer of epithelial cells lines each alveolus.

cards.title: 5.1.4 The Lungs
body: The branching network of bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli comprise the lungs.
Lungs are respiratory organs found in the thoracic cavity.
The left lung is slightly smaller (because of the heart that is located slightly to the left of the body) and has two lobes.
The right lung is bigger, with three lobes.

cards.title: 5.3 Cellular Respiration
body: **Cellular respiration** is a complex process of energy release from food in a cell.
Energy is released when simple sugar molecules are oxidized during a series of steps controlled by enzymes.
Respiration is initiated in the cytoplasm and completed in the mitochondria.
Respiration can be divided into two types, depending on the presence or absence of oxygen during the reaction.
**Glycolysis literally** means the “splitting of sugars”.

cards.title: Cellular Respiration
body: Gases move by diffusion: O₂ alveolus → blood; CO₂ blood → alveolus. In tissues the arrows reverse. Cellular respiration in mitochondria: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP. Exercise raises rate and depth because muscles demand more ATP and make more CO₂.

cards.title: More detail — air and ATP
body: Trachea rings are C-shaped so the oesophagus can bulge when you swallow. Alveoli: millions, moist, one-cell wall, wrapped in capillaries — four features every 4-mark wants. Smoking damages cilia and alveoli (emphysema = less surface).

Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and yields much ATP. Anaerobic in muscle: glucose → lactic acid + little ATP; oxygen debt afterwards. Plants / yeast anaerobic path is different (ethanol) — don’t mix unless asked. Exercise: more CO₂ in blood → brain raises breathing rate and heart rate together.

glossary.meaning: Exhalation is the process by which alveolar air is released out of the body.
Aerobic respiration is the release of energy from glucose or other organic substrate in the presence of oxygen.
External respiration (breathing) is the process of inhaling (breathing in oxygen) and exhaling (breathing out carbon dioxide) which occurs in the lungs.
The first stage of respiration, in the cytoplasm, in which glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvate, releasing a little ATP.
The movement of air into and out of the lungs (inhalation and exhalation) caused by the diaphragm and rib muscles.
Inhalation is the process by which atmospheric air is drawn into the body through the lungs.

questions.q: A biology class in Asmara is studying why oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged so rapidly inside the lungs. Which of the following combinations correctly states two structural adaptations of the alveoli that make this rapid diffusion possible?

options.A: A thick, multi-layered alveolar wall and a dry inner lining
options.B: A thin single-layer epithelial wall and a moist inner surface
options.C: Hard C-shaped cartilage rings around each alveolus and a moist inner surface
options.D: A dense network of capillaries and a thick, muscular alveolar wall

why: **Recall where exchange happens.** The unit states that the exchange of $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ occurs entirely within the alveoli, and that it takes place by simple diffusion.

**Check each stated adaptation.** The unit lists three adaptations of alveoli: extremely thin walls (a single layer of flat epithelial cells, giving a very short diffusion path), a moist inner surface (so gases dissolve in water first), and a massive surface area from about 600 to 700 million alveoli.

**Test the options.** Option A is wrong because the alveolar wall is one cell thick, not thick and multi-layered, and the surface is moist, not dry. Option C is wrong because cartilage rings belong to the trachea, not to alveoli. Option D is wrong because a thick muscular wall would lengthen the diffusion path.
**Conclude.** Option B alone names two genuine adaptations: the thin single-layer epithelial wall and the moist inner surface.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: During a hospital visit in Keren, a student is told that a patient's lungs contain roughly 600 to 700 million tiny air sacs. Which of the following best explains why this huge number of alveoli is important for the patient?
questions.answer: C. It creates a massive surface area for gas exchange by diffusion.
why: **Recall the third adaptation.** The unit states that the lungs contain approximately 600 to 700 million alveoli surrounded by a dense capillary network, providing a massive surface area for gas exchange.
**Link structure to function.** Simple diffusion is faster when more surface is available, so a large total alveolar surface increases the rate of $$O_2$$ uptake and $$CO_2$$ removal.

**Check the distractors.** Option A is wrong because surface area does not warm the air; warming and filtering happen in the nasal cavity. Option B is wrong because the total distance for diffusion is set by the thinness of the walls, not by the number of alveoli. Option D is wrong because the volume of each individual alveolus is microscopic, not large.
**Conclude.** The large number of alveoli matters because it maximises the surface area available for diffusion.

questions.q: A student in Massawa draws a diagram of an alveolus and labels the surrounding capillary. Which of the following explains why both the alveolar wall and the capillary wall are only one cell thick?

why: **Recall the first adaptation.** The unit states that the walls of both the alveoli and the surrounding capillaries consist of a single layer of flat epithelial cells, creating an incredibly short diffusion path.
**Relate thickness to diffusion.** The shorter the distance a gas must travel, the faster it diffuses across the membranes, so a one-cell-thick barrier speeds up $$O_2$$ and $$CO_2$$ movement.

**Eliminate the distractors.** Option B is wrong because thin walls do not generate the pressure that drives ventilation; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles do. Option C is wrong because mucus and cilia for trapping dust are found in the nasal cavity and airways. Option D is wrong because the air inside the alveoli is warm because the nose warmed it before it arrived, not because the wall is thin.
**Conclude.** The single-cell thickness exists to minimise the diffusion distance.

questions.q: In a school laboratory in Asmara, a group of Grade 10 students estimated that a small section of lung tissue they examined provided a total surface area for gaseous exchange of $$5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. The average surface area of a single alveolus is $$1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$. Calculate the number of alveoli present in that small section of lung tissue.
why: **Identify the given values.** Total surface area of the section $$= 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$. Average surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

**State the working formula.** Since the total surface area is supplied by many identical alveoli, the number of alveoli is found by dividing the total surface area by the surface area of one alveolus: $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{\text{Total surface area}}{\text{Surface area of one alveolus}}$$.
**Substitute the values.** $$\text{Number of alveoli} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-7}}$$.

**Carry out the arithmetic.** Dividing the coefficients gives $$5.0 \div 1.0 = 5.0$$, and dividing the powers of ten gives $$10^{-3} \div 10^{-7} = 10^{-3-(-7)} = 10^{4}$$. Therefore the number of alveoli $$= 5.0 \times 10^{4}$$.
**Conclude.** The small section of lung tissue contains $$5.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli, that is 50,000 alveoli, which shows how densely packed the gas-exchange surface is.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

why: **Identify the given values.** Total surface area $$= 8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$$ and surface area of one alveolus $$= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2$$.

**Conclude.** The sample contains $$8.0 \times 10^{4}$$ alveoli, that is 80,000 alveoli.

questions.q: A student in Asmara is revising quietly at her desk, while her brother is sprinting in a school athletics race. Explain which form of cellular respiration each of them mainly uses in their muscle cells, and compare the amount of ATP each pathway can release from one molecule of glucose.
questions.answer: The resting student's muscle cells mainly use aerobic respiration, which releases up to $$36\text{ to } 38\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule with oxygen, while the sprinting brother's muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), which releases only $$2\ \text{ATP}$$ per glucose molecule without oxygen, making aerobic respiration about 18 to 19 times more efficient.
why: **Define cellular respiration.** Cellular respiration is the enzymatic oxidation of glucose inside cells to produce ATP. Both aerobic and anaerobic pathways begin with glycolysis, the splitting of a glucose molecule into two pyruvic acid molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP.

**Identify the pathway used at rest.** While the student is resting quietly, oxygen is plentiful, so her muscle cells use aerobic respiration. Pyruvic acid enters the mitochondria and is completely broken down in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and up to 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Identify the pathway used during sprinting.** During intense exercise the oxygen supplied by the lungs and blood is insufficient to meet the high ATP demand. Her brother's muscle cells therefore switch to anaerobic respiration in the cytoplasm, converting pyruvic acid into lactic acid and releasing only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Compare the ATP yields.** Aerobic respiration yields about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose molecule, whereas anaerobic lactic acid fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose molecule, so aerobic respiration is roughly 18 to 19 times more efficient.

**Relate to the observations.** This explains why the sprinter's muscles tire quickly: lactic acid accumulation makes muscles stiff and sore, while the resting student's cells obtain far more ATP from the same amount of glucose using oxygen.

questions.q: A baker in Keren uses yeast to make bread dough rise, while a weightlifter in the same town performs a very heavy lift. State the type of respiration each process depends on and name the products formed from glucose in each case.
questions.answer: The yeast carries out anaerobic respiration (alcohol fermentation), producing ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide with 2 ATP per glucose; the weightlifter's muscle cells carry out anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation), producing lactic acid with 2 ATP per glucose.
why: **Recall the two anaerobic pathways.** The unit describes alcohol fermentation in plants, yeast and some bacteria, and lactic acid fermentation in animal muscle cells during intense exercise.

**Identify the yeast process.** In bread making, yeast converts glucose into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, and this carbon dioxide is what makes the dough rise. The energy released is only 2 ATP per glucose molecule.

**Identify the weightlifter's process.** During a very heavy lift the oxygen supply to the muscles is insufficient, so pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid, releasing 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
**Conclude with products.** Yeast: ethyl alcohol, carbon dioxide and 2 ATP. Muscle: lactic acid and 2 ATP. Both occur in the absence of oxygen.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Explain why the lungs alone cannot move air in and out, and state which structures provide the force for breathing.
questions.answer: Lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they cannot pump air by themselves; breathing is driven by pressure differences created by the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.
why: **Describe the lung tissue.** The unit states that lungs are soft, elastic and non-muscular, so they contain no skeletal muscle of their own and cannot actively expand or contract.
**Explain the driving force.** Breathing is driven by pressure differences created by two sets of muscles: the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.

**Link muscle action to air flow.** On inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles pull the ribs up and out, increasing thoracic volume and lowering alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows in; on exhalation these muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases and air is pushed out.
**Conclude.** The lungs are passive; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles change the volume of the thoracic cavity and create the pressure gradients that ventilate the lungs.

units.title: The Excretory System
units.intro:
Excretion removes *metabolic* waste (CO₂, urea, excess salts and water). Egestion is undigested food — different word.

Organs: lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat: salts, a little urea), liver (makes urea from amino acids — deamination), kidneys (filter blood, keep what you still need).

cards.title: 6.1 The Excretory Products
body: All cells carry out metabolic reactions.
If these substances accumulate in the fluid surrounding the cells, they would become toxic (poisonous) and upset the homeostasis of the organism.
Single-celled organisms can remove their waste products by simple diffusion, but large animals require a more elaborate excretory system.
The external environment of a living organism is constantly changing.
The internal environment of the cells (the amount of water, the concentration of glucose, the temperature, etc.) is kept almost constant all the time.

body: Urea comes from surplus amino acids: liver strips the nitrogen (deamination) and makes urea, which is less toxic than ammonia. Bladder stores; sphincter is learned control.
Dialysis mimics the filter when both kidneys fail. Sweat cools you (Grade 11 temperature) and happens to carry some urea — it is not the main urea door.

tips.text: All cells constantly carry out metabolic reactions. These metabolic reactions produce waste products.
The main metabolic wastes in most mammals are carbon dioxide, excess water and salt, urea and red pigments.
Carbon dioxide and excess water are produced during cellular respiration.
The amino acids not used as a source of energy are catabolized in the liver by a process called deamination.
The nitrogen-containing part of the excess amino acid is combined with carbon dioxide and converted into urea, ammonia and uric acid.
The urea dissolves in the blood plasma and is taken to the kidneys to be excreted.
The liver also has many other functions.
The excretory system is responsible for the maintenance of homeostasis by selectively adjusting the concentration of substances in blood and other body fluids.

If allowed to accumulate, metabolic wastes would eventually reach toxic concentrations and upset the homeostasis of the organism. These waste products must, therefore, be removed from the body regularly by the process of excretion.

The excretory organs in mammals are the skin, lungs, kidneys and liver. However, the kidneys are the main excretory organs because they excrete nitrogenous wastes, excess water and mineral salts, and other substances in the form of urine.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes excretion from egestion (defecation) in a mammal?

options.A: Excretion removes undigested food that has passed through the alimentary canal, while egestion removes urea made in the liver.
options.B: Excretion removes metabolic wastes produced by chemical reactions inside the body cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.
options.C: Excretion removes only sweat and bile pigments, while egestion removes carbon dioxide and urea.
options.D: Excretion and egestion both remove the chemical waste products formed by reactions inside the body cells.

why: **Recall the definition of excretion.** Excretion is the biological process by which metabolic waste products, produced by chemical reactions inside the cells of the body, are removed. Typical examples are carbon dioxide, excess water and urea, and the process helps to maintain homeostasis.

**Recall the definition of egestion.** Egestion (defecation) is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that has simply passed through the alimentary canal and leaves the body as faeces. Like the empty grocery boxes in the house-cleaning analogy, this material never became part of the cells' activities.

**Test each option against the two definitions.** A reverses the two processes, so it is wrong. C is wrong because excretion also removes carbon dioxide and urea, not only sweat and bile pigments, and because egestion removes faeces, not carbon dioxide and urea. D is wrong because the materials removed by egestion were never products of reactions inside the cells.

**Select the one correct statement.** Only B matches the definitions exactly: excretion removes metabolic wastes made inside the cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A student in Asmara claims that defecation is a form of excretion because both processes remove unwanted material from the body. Correct the student's statement using the biological definitions of excretion and egestion.
questions.answer: Defecation (egestion) is not excretion. Egestion is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that passed through the alimentary canal and never entered the body cells, whereas excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes such as carbon dioxide, excess water and urea that were produced by chemical reactions inside the cells. Only the second process is excretion.
why: **State what excretion removes.** Excretion removes metabolic waste products (for example carbon dioxide, excess water and urea) that are formed by chemical reactions inside the cells, and it maintains homeostasis.
**State what egestion removes.** Egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal as faeces; this material passed through the gut without taking part in cell metabolism.

**Correct the student.** Because faeces are not products of chemical reactions inside the cells, defecation cannot be called excretion. The two processes differ in the origin of the material removed, not merely in the route by which it leaves the body.

**Classify the options.** A, C and D are all unabsorbed materials that simply pass along the alimentary canal, so they are removed by egestion. Urea, however, is made in the liver by deamination and is a metabolic waste carried in the blood plasma.
**Conclude.** Urea is the only listed material that is a product of cell metabolism, so B is the correct answer.

(b) The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the ______. (c) The single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body is the ______.
why: **Recall the structure of the nephron.** The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney and consists of the glomerulus enclosed in the Bowman's capsule, plus the renal tubule.

**Recall the exit tube.** The urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside during urination; the ureters, by contrast, bring urine to the bladder.
**State the answers.** (a) glomerulus; (b) nephron; (c) urethra.

questions.q: During a hot afternoon shift on the salt flats near Massawa, a labourer loses $$3.2\ \text{liters}$$ of sweat. In this sweat, mineral salts (NaCl) make up $$0.30\%$$ of the mass and urea makes up $$0.05\%$$ of the mass. Given that $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$ and that $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost, (b) the mass of urea lost, and (c) the total mass of these two substances lost in the sweat.
questions.answer: (a) $$9.6\ \text{g}$$ of mineral salts; (b) $$1.6\ \text{g}$$ of urea; (c) $$11.2\ \text{g}$$ in total.
why: **Convert the volume of sweat into a mass.** The volume is $$3.2\ \text{L} = 3.2 \times 1000 = 3200\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the total mass of sweat is $$3200\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 3200\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of mineral salts.** Mineral salts are $$0.30\%$$ of the mass, so mass of salts $$= \frac{0.30}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0030 \times 3200 = 9.6\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of urea.** Urea is $$0.05\%$$ of the mass, so mass of urea $$= \frac{0.05}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0005 \times 3200 = 1.6\ \text{g}$$.
**Add the two masses.** Total mass lost $$= 9.6\ \text{g} + 1.6\ \text{g} = 11.2\ \text{g}$$.

**Interpret the result biologically.** The sweat glands in the dermis have removed water, mineral salts and a small amount of urea from the blood. This shows the skin acting both as an organ of excretion (removing metabolic waste) and as a means of cooling the body by evaporation.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A student in Asmara walks home quickly on a warm afternoon and loses $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of sweat. The sweat contains $$0.25\%$$ mineral salts and $$0.04\%$$ urea by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost and (b) the mass of urea lost.
why: **Convert the volume of sweat to mass.** $$0.8\ \text{L} = 800\ \text{mL}$$, and since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the mass of sweat is $$800\ \text{g}$$.
**Find the mass of mineral salts.** Mass of salts $$= 0.25\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.25}{100} \times 800 = 2.0\ \text{g}$$.
**Find the mass of urea.** Mass of urea $$= 0.04\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.04}{100} \times 800 = 0.32\ \text{g}$$.
**State the conclusion.** The smaller sweat loss removes $$2.0\ \text{g}$$ of salts and $$0.32\ \text{g}$$ of urea, still showing that sweat carries away mineral salts and a trace of metabolic waste.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A healthy adult living in Keren excretes $$1.5\ \text{L}$$ of urine in one day. The urine contains $$2.0\%$$ urea and $$0.9\%$$ mineral salts by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of urine as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate the total mass of dissolved waste (urea plus mineral salts) excreted in the urine that day.
questions.answer: $$43.5\ \text{g}$$ in total ($$30\ \text{g}$$ urea and $$13.5\ \text{g}$$ mineral salts).
why: **Convert the urine volume into a mass.** $$1.5\ \text{L} = 1500\ \text{mL}$$, so the mass of urine is $$1500\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 1500\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of urea.** Mass of urea $$= \frac{2.0}{100} \times 1500 = 30\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of mineral salts.** Mass of salts $$= \frac{0.9}{100} \times 1500 = 13.5\ \text{g}$$.
**Add the two masses.** Total dissolved waste $$= 30\ \text{g} + 13.5\ \text{g} = 43.5\ \text{g}$$, all of it carried in the urine formed by the kidneys.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A camel kept near the hot coastal town of Massawa can go for many days with very little drinking water, while a dairy cow kept in the cool highlands of Asmara must drink frequently. Using the structure of the nephron and the process of osmoregulation, explain how the camel's extensive, extremely long loop of Henle allows it to survive on so little water.
questions.answer: The camel's very long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla and maintains a steep concentration gradient there, so a large amount of water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood. The camel therefore produces a small volume of highly concentrated urine and loses very little water. The cow's shorter loop of Henle produces only a small gradient, so less water is reabsorbed, more dilute urine is formed, and the cow must drink frequently.
why: **Recall where water is reabsorbed in the nephron.** The unit states that in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, and that the loop of Henle is the region responsible for osmoregulation (water balance).

**Relate loop length to the concentration gradient.** The camel's extremely long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla of the kidney. Because the loop is so long, it builds and maintains a very steep concentration gradient in the medulla.

**Explain the osmotic movement of water.** The steep gradient draws water out of the collecting duct and back into the surrounding blood capillaries by osmosis, so a very large proportion of the water in the filtrate is returned to the blood instead of being lost.

**Link this to the volume and concentration of urine.** Because so much water is reabsorbed, the camel produces only a small volume of highly concentrated urine. Its water loss is therefore minimised, which is the advantage needed in a dry desert environment.

**Contrast with the cow.** The cow has a much shorter loop of Henle, so only a small concentration gradient is maintained in the medulla. Less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, more dilute urine is produced in a larger volume, and the cow must therefore drink frequently to replace the water it loses.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon in Massawa a worker sweats heavily and produces only a small volume of concentrated urine, but on a cool morning in Asmara the same worker produces a larger volume of dilute urine. Explain this difference in terms of osmoregulation in the nephron.
questions.answer: Heavy sweating removes a large volume of water from the blood, so the blood becomes more concentrated. In the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, more water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, leaving a small volume of highly concentrated urine. On the cool morning little water is lost by sweating, less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, and a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. In this way the nephron keeps the water content of the body constant.
why: **State the effect of heavy sweating.** Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating on a hot day removes a large amount of water from the blood and body fluids.
**Locate the site of water reabsorption.** Water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, with the loop of Henle responsible for osmoregulation.

**Explain the hot-day response.** Because the blood has lost water, more water is drawn back from the filtrate by osmosis, so a small volume of highly concentrated urine is formed and water is conserved.

**Explain the cool-day response and conclude.** With little water lost by sweating, less reabsorption by osmosis is needed, so a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. The nephron therefore maintains a constant internal water balance (homeostasis).
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Describe the two main processes that take place in a nephron, ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption, stating clearly where each occurs and what each achieves.
questions.answer: Ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, creating high blood pressure that forces water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea out of the capillaries into the Bowman's capsule to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins remain in the blood. Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule: all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are actively transported back into the surrounding blood capillaries, so useful materials are not lost from the body.
why: **Define ultrafiltration and give its site.** Ultrafiltration is high-pressure physical filtering that occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.

**Explain how the pressure is produced.** The afferent arteriole entering the glomerulus is wider than the efferent arteriole leaving it, which creates high blood pressure inside the glomerular capillaries.

**State what passes through and what is held back.** Water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea are forced out to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins are too large to pass through the pores and stay in the blood.

**Define selective reabsorption and give its site.** Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, where all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are taken back into the blood capillaries by active transport.

**State what is achieved.** Together the two processes remove nitrogenous waste and excess water and salts from the blood while returning useful materials such as glucose and amino acids to the body, which is why glucose is absent from the urine of a healthy person.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Both kidneys of a healthy adult living in Asmara produce about $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate every day. During one particular day this adult excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.35\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from the body on that day. (b) Express this total fluid loss as a percentage of the daily volume of glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain, using the events in the nephron, why the volume of fluid actually lost is so much smaller than the volume of filtrate produced.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$1.58\%$$ of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Over $$99\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood because glucose, amino acids and essential mineral salts are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct; only a small volume is finally excreted as urine, sweat and water vapour.
why: **List the measured fluid losses.** Urine $$= 1.6\ \text{L}$$, sweat $$= 0.9\ \text{L}$$ and water vapour in expired air $$= 0.35\ \text{L}$$. All three are measured in the same unit, so they can be added directly.
**Calculate the total volume lost (part a).** Total volume lost $$= 1.6\ \text{L} + 0.9\ \text{L} + 0.35\ \text{L} = 2.85\ \text{L}$$.
**Set up the percentage calculation (part b).** Percentage lost $$= \frac{\text{total volume lost}}{\text{volume of glomerular filtrate}} \times 100 = \frac{2.85}{180} \times 100$$.

**Complete the arithmetic.** $$\frac{2.85}{180} = 0.01583$$, and $$0.01583 \times 100 = 1.583\%$$, which rounds to approximately $$1.58\%$$. This means well over $$98\%$$ of the filtrate never leaves the body.

**Explain the fate of the filtrate in the nephron (part c).** As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are returned to the surrounding blood capillaries by active transport (selective reabsorption). In the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, water is reabsorbed by osmosis. More than $$99\%$$ of the filtered water is therefore returned to the blood.

**Link the explanation to the numbers.** Of the $$180\ \text{L}$$ filtered, only $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ leaves as urine, so about $$178.4\ \text{L}$$ is reabsorbed. The remaining losses as sweat and water vapour are small additional losses from the body fluids. This high efficiency of reabsorption is what allows the body to lose only about $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ from a filtrate volume of $$180\ \text{L}$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Both kidneys of a labourer working in Massawa produce $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate in one day. On that day he excretes $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$2.4\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.45\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from his body. (b) Express this total as a percentage of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain why sweating heavily on a hot day leads to the production of a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
questions.answer: (a) $$3.75\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$2.08\%$$ of the glomerular filtrate. (c) Heavy sweating removes water from the blood; in response, more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood, so a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced and water is conserved.
why: **Add the three fluid losses.** Total volume lost $$= 0.9\ \text{L} + 2.4\ \text{L} + 0.45\ \text{L} = 3.75\ \text{L}$$.
**Set up the percentage.** Percentage lost $$= \frac{3.75}{180} \times 100$$.

**Complete the arithmetic.** $$\frac{3.75}{180} = 0.02083$$, so the percentage is $$2.083\%$$, approximately $$2.08\%$$. Even with heavy sweating, more than $$97\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood.

**Explain the effect of sweating on urine.** Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating lowers the water content of the blood. More water is then reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, leaving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

**Conclude on osmoregulation.** The kidney adjusts the volume of water reabsorbed so that the water content of the body stays constant; this is osmoregulation, and it protects the body from dehydration on a hot day.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A nurse in Asmara records the fluid output of a patient over two days. On the cool day the patient forms $$180\ \text{L}$$ of glomerular filtrate and excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine; on the hot day the same volume of filtrate is formed, but only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of urine is excreted. (a) Calculate the volume of filtrate returned to the blood on each day. (b) Explain, using the nephron, why less urine is formed on the hot day.
questions.answer: (a) Cool day: $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. Hot day: $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. (b) On the hot day more water is lost from the body, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the collecting duct back into the blood, leaving less water in the filtrate and therefore a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
why: **State the relationship between filtrate, urine and reabsorption.** Volume reabsorbed $$=$$ volume of glomerular filtrate $$-$$ volume of urine excreted.
**Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the cool day.** $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{178.4}{180} \times 100 = 99.1\%$$ of the filtrate.
**Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the hot day.** $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{179.2}{180} \times 100 = 99.6\%$$ of the filtrate.

**Explain the difference using the nephron.** The loop of Henle maintains a concentration gradient in the medulla, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. On the hot day the body has lost more water, so a greater proportion is reabsorbed and only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of concentrated urine remains to be excreted.

units.title: The Sense Organs
units.intro:
Receptors turn a stimulus into a nerve impulse. Skin: touch, pressure, pain, temperature. Nose: chemoreceptors in the air stream. Tongue: taste buds (sweet, salt, sour, bitter — umami may be named). Eye: cornea + lens focus on the retina; rods = dim/black-white; cones = colour in bright light; iris controls pupil. Ear: pinna → canal → drum → ossicles → cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance).

Internal receptors watch stretch, blood chemistry, posture — they feed homeostasis in Grade 11.

cards.title: More detail — eye and ear
body: Eye path: cornea does most of the bending, lens does the fine focus (accommodation: fat lens for near, thin for far). Iris circular and radial muscles set pupil size. Blind spot = optic nerve exit, no receptors. Short sight: long eyeball, image in front of retina, diverging lens. Long sight: short eyeball or stiff lens, converging lens.

Ear path: air waves → drum → three bones amplify → oval window → fluid in cochlea → hair cells → auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation (fluid lag). Eustachian tube equalises pressure with the throat.

cards.title: 7.1.1 The Skin
body: **The skin** is the sense organ which covers the whole body.
For example the fingertips, lips and cheeks have the greatest concentration of receptors and are, therefore, more sensitive to their respective stimuli.
Skin receptors receive a signal and transmit it via nerve cells to the brain.
In the brain, the signals are interpreted as sensations.

cards.title: 7.1.2 The Nose
body: The nasal cavity is lined with mucous membranes that have smell receptors, which are connected to the olfactory nerve.
The smell itself consists of vapours of various substances.
The smell receptors are sensitive to different types of sensations and interact with the molecules of various vapours, transmitting the sensations to the brain through the olfactory bulb.
The chemical molecules of any odorous substance that enter the nose dissolve in the mucus and stimulate the olfactory receptors.

cards.title: 7.1.3 The Tongue
body: **The tongue** is a sense organ that helps identify taste.
The human tongue is dotted with thousands of taste buds, which are made up of many receptor cells.
Many of the taste buds are found in large swellings, called papillae.
Generally, the taste buds close to the tip of the tongue are sensitive to sweet tastes, whereas those at the back respond to bitter tastes.

cards.title: 7.1.4 The Eye
body: Human eyes are situated in the eye sockets of the skull.
The sockets give protection to the eyes.
A number of muscles hold the eyes in place, enabling them to move in different directions.
The front of the eyeball is covered by a thin, transparent membrane, the conjunctiva.

cards.title: 7.1.5 The Ear
body: **The ear** is the sense organ that assists in hearing.
The external ear: The external ear consists of the pinna, auditory canal and eardrum (tympanum).
The pinna helps to direct sound waves into the auditory canal.
Glands in the walls of the auditory canal produce a waxy material.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.
**Steps:**
The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube in the human ear?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures of the middle ear.
**Concepts:** The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the pharynx, allowing air to pass in and out to equalize pressure across the eardrum.
**Steps:**
Sound amplification is done by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).
Equalization of pressure prevents the eardrum from rupturing or dampening vibrations, which is mediated by the Eustachian tube.

cards.answer: Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In bright light conditions, which of the following pupillary muscular actions occurs?

options.A: Radial muscles contract, dilating the pupil
options.B: Circular muscles contract, constricting the pupil
options.C: Radial muscles relax, constricting the pupil
options.D: Circular muscles relax, dilating the pupil

cards.why:
**Given:** Pupillary response to high light intensity.

**Concepts:** The iris contains antagonistic muscles. In bright light, parasympathetic stimulation causes the circular (sphincter) muscles to contract, reducing pupil diameter to limit light entry.

**Steps:**
1. Bright light requires pupillary constriction.
2. Constriction is executed by the contraction of circular muscles.
3. Dilation (in dim light) is executed by the contraction of radial muscles.

**Final Result:** **Circular muscles contract, constricting the pupil** is the correct anatomical reflex.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which area of the retina lacks rod cells entirely, consists exclusively of cone cells, and serves as the point of maximum visual acuity?
cards.why:
**Given:** Visual acuity regions of the retina.

**Concepts:** The fovea centralis (yellow spot) contains a high density of cone photoreceptors and no rod cells, making it the center of sharpest vision.

**Steps:**
1. The blind spot (optic disc) lacks both rods and cones where axons exit.
2. The fovea is located at the center of the retina and contains only cones.
3. Highly concentrated cones facilitate maximal resolution.

**Final Result:** **Fovea Centralis (Yellow Spot)** is the site of maximum visual acuity.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Constriction and dilation of the eye pupil is associated with the
cards.why: The **iris** is the colored part of the eye. It contains circular and radial muscles that control the size of the **pupil**. By constricting (getting smaller) or dilating (getting larger), the iris regulates the amount of light entering the eye.

cards.title: 7.2 The Internal Receptors
body: Receptors that receive information about internal body conditions are called **internal receptors**.
Organisms receive information about a stimulus or changes within their body with the help of these receptors.
Internal receptors detect stimuli related to muscle length and tension, limb position, pain, blood composition, blood volume, blood pressure, body temperature, etc.
Internal receptors can be classified as mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors and chemoreceptors.
Mechanoreceptors are specialized receptors that monitor pressure, stretching, and bending forces.

cards.title: Explain how internal receptors keep the body informed
cards.problem: A person stands up quickly and feels dizzy for a moment, then recovers. Explain the role of internal receptors.

steps.text: **Step 1: Name the change.** Standing quickly lowers blood pressure in the head for a moment.
**Step 2: Name the receptors.** Pressure receptors (baroreceptors – a kind of mechanoreceptor) in the aorta and carotid arteries detect the fall.
**Step 3: Message.** They send impulses to the brain (medulla).
**Step 4: Response.** The brain raises the heart rate and narrows blood vessels, so blood pressure returns to normal and the dizziness passes.

cards.answer: Baroreceptors (internal mechanoreceptors) detect the drop in blood pressure and signal the brain, which raises heart rate and constricts vessels to restore pressure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?
cards.why:
**Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.

**Steps:**
1. The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
2. The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.
3. The conjunctiva is the superficial mucous membrane that protects the cornea from friction.

**Final Result:** **Conjunctiva** is the correct structure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube in the human ear?

options.B: Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane
options.C: Transmission of neural impulses to the auditory cortex
options.D: Maintenance of dynamic and static bodily equilibrium

cards.why:
**Given:** Anatomical structures of the middle ear.

**Concepts:** The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the pharynx, allowing air to pass in and out to equalize pressure across the eardrum.

**Steps:**
1. Sound amplification is done by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).
2. Equalization of pressure prevents the eardrum from rupturing or dampening vibrations, which is mediated by the Eustachian tube.
3. Neural transmission is done by the auditory nerve.

**Final Result:** **Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane** is the primary function.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All of the following stimuli are detected **only** by skin, except
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The skin contains various receptors: Mechanoreceptors (pressure), Nociceptors (pain), and Thermoreceptors (hot/cold).
**Step 2:** All the listed stimuli (A, B, C, D) are primary sensations detected by the skin.
**Step 3:** Since all are detected by the skin, 'none' of them is an exception in this context.

glossary.meaning: An eye disease in which the lens becomes cloudy, blurring vision.
The three tiny bones of the middle ear (hammer, anvil, stirrup) that pass and amplify vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear.

tips.text: Humans are equipped with internal and external receptors that help them respond to changes in their body and the environment. These receptors are very important in the survival of the organism.
Some of the receptors form sense organs like the skin, nose, tongue, eye and ear. These sense organs respond to different stimuli in the environment.
The sense organs and stimuli they respond to are listed below.
Receptors which recognize different sensations, like pain, touch, pressure, etc. are present in the skin.
The nose is the sense organ where olfactory receptors are present.
Receptors, which recognize the primary tastes such as sweet, sour, bitter and salty, are present in the tongue.
The eye is the sense organ that helps us to see objects in our surroundings.
Images in the eye are formed on the retina, where rod and cone cells (the photoreceptors) are located.
The structures of the human ear assist in hearing sound.
The malfunctioning and non-functioning of sense organs are hazardous to one’s health. Therefore, we should take precautions for their care and proper functioning.
